question: Is a named person accountable for software licensing, renewals and license compliance?
level_0: No one is accountable; renewals and true-ups are handled by whoever receives the vendor's or reseller's email.
level_1: An IT staff member handles Microsoft licensing informally alongside other duties; responsibilities are not written down and finance signs contracts separately.
level_2: A SAM owner is named for Microsoft licensing, but clinical application licenses, renewals and audit requests sit with different people and no RACI exists.
level_3: A named SAM owner with a documented backup holds written responsibilities across IT, procurement, finance and compliance (RACI), covering Microsoft and the major clinical vendors.
target_state: The SAM owner reports licensing KPIs to leadership at least quarterly, the RACI is reviewed annually, and the backup has prepared at least one renewal or true-up.
evidence: RACI, charter or job description naming the SAM owner and backup — IT governance or HR documents. | The last two renewal or true-up packages showing who prepared, reviewed and approved them — procurement or finance files. | Contract owner list for every software vendor — contract management system or contract spreadsheet.
recommended_action: Name a SAM owner with a backup and publish a RACI covering IT, finance, procurement, compliance and clinical application contracts.
probing_questions: Who prepared the counts for the last Microsoft renewal or true-up, and who signed it? | If a vendor audit letter arrived tomorrow, who would respond and who would they involve? | Who owns licensing for the EHR, imaging (PACS), laboratory and revenue cycle systems? | What happens to licensing decisions when that person is on leave or leaves the organization?
red_flags: The named owner cannot state the date of the next Microsoft renewal or anniversary. | Ownership is assigned to "the reseller" or "the MSP" with no internal accountable person.
healthcare_considerations: In small hospitals the CFO or purchasing office often signs software contracts while a two- or three-person IT team runs the tenant; without a bridging owner, true-ups are signed on reseller-supplied counts. | Clinical application licenses are frequently bundled into EHR, PACS or laboratory vendor contracts managed by the department or the health information management office, outside IT's view.
action_to_2: Name an interim SAM owner and list every software vendor with its contract owner (days).
action_to_3: Publish a RACI across IT, finance, procurement and compliance and assign a trained backup (weeks).
action_to_4: Add licensing KPIs to quarterly leadership reporting and review the RACI annually (months).

question: Are licensing decisions governed by a documented policy (requests, approvals, reharvesting, retirement)?
level_0: No policy exists; licenses are bought or assigned on request by whoever has admin rights.
level_1: Unwritten habits exist (for example, "ask IT first"), but purchases also happen on departmental credit cards and through vendor portals.
level_2: A draft or partial policy covers Microsoft 365 requests, but not reharvesting, retirement, SaaS purchases or clinical application licenses.
level_3: An approved policy defines request, approval, assignment, reharvesting and retirement for all software, and tickets show it is followed for new purchases and departures.
target_state: Policy compliance is measured (for example, purchases outside the process, time to reharvest), exceptions are logged and approved, and the policy is reviewed annually.
evidence: Approved software licensing policy with version and approval date — policy library. | Sample of five recent license request tickets showing approval and assignment — service desk. | Card or accounts-payable report of software purchases outside procurement — finance.
recommended_action: Approve a licensing policy covering request, approval, assignment, reharvesting and retirement for all software, enforced through the service desk.
probing_questions: Walk me through the last license request: who asked, who approved, how was it assigned and recorded? | Can a department buy a SaaS tool or extra seats on a credit card or through a vendor portal without IT knowing? | What does the policy say should happen to a license when a user leaves, changes role or goes inactive? | When was the policy last approved, and by whom?
red_flags: The policy exists but no ticket references it. | Licenses are assigned directly in the admin center with no request record.
healthcare_considerations: Medical staff, residents, students and agency staff join and leave on different calendars than employees; the policy must state who requests and removes licenses for each group (HR, medical staff office, education coordinator). | Departments such as radiology, laboratory and pharmacy often buy add-on modules directly from clinical vendors; require these purchases to pass through the same approval and recording step.
action_to_2: Write a one-page request and approval rule for Microsoft 365 and enforce it through the service desk (weeks).
action_to_3: Extend the policy to reharvesting, retirement, SaaS and clinical application purchases and get it approved (one to two months).
action_to_4: Measure off-process purchases and reharvest time and review the policy annually (months).

question: Are renewals tracked in a calendar and reviewed well before expiry?
level_0: Renewal dates are unknown until an invoice or an auto-renewal notice arrives.
level_1: The Microsoft renewal date is known, but clinical and SaaS renewals are not tracked and usage review starts within the last month.
level_2: A renewal list exists for major contracts, but review starts less than 90 days before expiry and auto-renewal and notice clauses are not recorded.
level_3: Every agreement is in a renewal calendar with notice periods and auto-renewal terms, and usage and needs are reviewed at least six months before each major renewal.
target_state: Renewal preparation follows a standard timeline (for example 9, 6 and 3 months), outcomes are compared with targets, and lessons feed the next renewal.
evidence: Renewal calendar listing agreement, term end, notice period and auto-renewal status — contract register. | Subscription term end dates and renewal settings — Microsoft 365 admin center (Billing > Your products) or the reseller portal. | Minutes or notes from the last renewal review showing the start date — procurement files.
recommended_action: Keep a renewal calendar with notice dates for every contract and start Microsoft renewal reviews at least six months before term end.
probing_questions: When does your Microsoft agreement or subscription term end, and what is the last date to reduce quantities or change plans? | Which contracts auto-renew, and what notice period applies? | For the last renewal, when did preparation start and what changed as a result? | Where are the EHR, PACS and other clinical renewal dates recorded?
red_flags: Annual-term subscriptions auto-renewed at the same quantity although headcount changed. | "The reseller reminds us" is the only tracking mechanism.
healthcare_considerations: Budget cycles in hospitals are often fixed months in advance; a renewal reviewed after the budget is set cannot fund a plan change or security add-on. | Clinical vendor contracts often have long notice periods and multi-year terms tied to support for regulated workflows; miss the notice window and the hospital is locked in for another term.
action_to_2: Build a renewal calendar for all Microsoft, SaaS and clinical contracts with term end and notice dates (weeks).
action_to_3: Start usage and needs review at least six months before each major renewal (next renewal cycle).
action_to_4: Adopt a 9-6-3 month renewal timeline and record outcomes against targets (months).

question: Is licensing cost reported to leadership with trends and per-user metrics?
level_0: Licensing cost is visible only as invoice lines in the general ledger.
level_1: IT can total annual licensing spend on request, but no regular report exists.
level_2: An annual licensing total is reported in the budget, without per-user cost, trend or waste figures.
level_3: Leadership receives at least a semiannual report showing licensing cost by vendor, cost per user, unassigned and inactive licenses, and savings achieved.
target_state: The report is produced at least quarterly from reconciled data, includes targets and trends, and leadership uses it in budget and renewal decisions.
evidence: Last licensing report presented to leadership — board, finance committee or IT steering pack. | Data behind the report (license counts, invoices) and the date it was reconciled — SAM owner's workbook.
recommended_action: Report licensing cost, cost per user, unused licenses and realized savings to leadership at least semiannually from reconciled data.
probing_questions: What did the organization spend on software licenses last year, and how was the number produced? | What is your cost per user per month for Microsoft 365, and how has it moved over two years? | Has leadership ever changed a decision because of a licensing report?
red_flags: Reported savings are list-price estimates, not invoice changes. | Per-user cost is calculated on total headcount instead of licensed users.
healthcare_considerations: Rural and critical access hospitals operate on thin margins; showing licensing cost per user next to the security gaps it could fund makes reinvestment decisions possible. | Separate employed staff, contracted clinicians and affiliated physician practices in the metrics; mixing them hides who is consuming licenses.
action_to_2: Produce a one-page annual licensing cost summary by vendor from invoices (weeks).
action_to_3: Add cost per user, unassigned and inactive licenses, and savings, reported at least semiannually (one quarter).
action_to_4: Report quarterly from reconciled data with targets and link it to budget and renewal decisions (months).

question: Is there a complete, current record of all Microsoft entitlements (agreements, products, quantities, terms)?
level_0: Nobody can say which Microsoft agreements are active or how many licenses were purchased.
level_1: Quantities are read from the admin center when needed; agreement numbers, terms and perpetual on-premises licenses are not recorded.
level_2: A spreadsheet lists cloud subscriptions and quantities, but perpetual licenses, Software Assurance, server and SQL Server licensing and term dates are incomplete.
level_3: One register lists every Microsoft agreement, product, quantity, term, channel (EA, CSP, MCA) and Software Assurance status, updated after each purchase and matched to the admin center.
target_state: The register is reconciled automatically or monthly against the admin center, reseller portal and invoices, and discrepancies are tracked to closure.
evidence: Entitlement register with agreement numbers, products, quantities and terms — SAM owner's repository. | Product and license counts — Microsoft 365 admin center, Billing > Your products and Licenses. | Volume licensing summary for perpetual licenses and Software Assurance — Microsoft 365 admin center volume licensing section or reseller statement.
recommended_action: Build one Microsoft entitlement register covering cloud subscriptions, perpetual server and SQL Server licenses, Software Assurance, quantities and terms.
probing_questions: Which agreements do you have with Microsoft or through a reseller today, and how did you confirm that? | Do you own perpetual Windows Server or SQL Server licenses, and is Software Assurance active on them? | Are there subscriptions bought by another department or a former reseller in a different billing account? | How many licenses of each product were purchased versus showing in the admin center?
red_flags: The register shows only cloud subscriptions; on-premises server and SQL Server licenses are "in a box somewhere". | Counts in the register were copied from the admin center, not from purchase records.
healthcare_considerations: On-premises EHR, interface engine and PACS servers often run Windows Server and SQL Server; entitlements for these are the most common gap and the largest compliance exposure. | Mergers, affiliations and former management companies leave behind separate tenants or agreements; ask about every legal entity and clinic.
action_to_2: Export current subscriptions and licenses from the admin center and reseller portal into one register (days).
action_to_3: Add perpetual, server, SQL Server and Software Assurance entitlements with agreement numbers and terms (weeks).
action_to_4: Reconcile the register monthly against portals and invoices and track discrepancies (months).

question: Are entitlements reconciled against contracts and invoices at least annually?
level_0: Invoices are paid without comparing them with what was ordered or used.
level_1: Someone checks an invoice when the total looks unusual.
level_2: Microsoft invoices are compared with the entitlement register once, but clinical and SaaS invoices are not, and discrepancies stay open.
level_3: At least annually, entitlements, contracts and invoices are reconciled for all major vendors, and each discrepancy is resolved with the supplier and recorded.
target_state: Reconciliation runs at least quarterly with a documented method, credits and corrections are tracked, and recurring causes are fixed at the source.
evidence: Last reconciliation workbook with entitlement, invoice and assignment columns — SAM owner. | Supplier correspondence or credit notes resulting from reconciliation — procurement or accounts payable.
recommended_action: Reconcile entitlements, contracts, invoices and assignments for all major vendors at least annually and resolve discrepancies with suppliers.
probing_questions: When did you last compare what you were billed with what you ordered and what is assigned? | What discrepancies did you find, and were credits obtained? | Do you get invoices for products nobody recognizes?
red_flags: Reconciliation compares invoices only with the reseller's own report. | No discrepancies have ever been found.
healthcare_considerations: Clinical vendors often bill by metrics such as beds, encounters, studies or providers; reconcile against the operational count from the relevant department, not last year's invoice. | Grant- or program-funded licenses (for example, telehealth) may have separate invoices and end dates that must be tracked.
action_to_2: Reconcile the last twelve months of Microsoft invoices against the entitlement register (weeks).
action_to_3: Reconcile all major vendors annually and resolve each discrepancy with the supplier (one quarter).
action_to_4: Reconcile quarterly with a documented method and fix recurring causes (months).

question: Are licenses for clinical and business applications (EHR modules, imaging, laboratory, revenue cycle) inventoried in the same repository?
level_0: Clinical application licenses are known only to the vendor and the department that uses them.
level_1: Contracts are filed, but license metrics, quantities and renewal dates are not extracted.
level_2: The EHR is recorded, but imaging, laboratory, pharmacy, revenue cycle and departmental SaaS licenses are missing or incomplete.
level_3: Clinical and business application licenses are recorded in the same repository as Microsoft licenses with metric, quantity, renewal date and owner.
target_state: Application licenses are reconciled at least annually against usage or operational counts and linked to the application inventory used for modernization planning.
evidence: License repository extract showing clinical and business applications with metrics — SAM owner. | Contract schedules or order forms for the EHR and two other clinical systems — contract files.
recommended_action: Record clinical and business application licenses with metric, quantity, renewal date and owner in the same repository as Microsoft licenses.
probing_questions: How is your EHR licensed (per bed, provider, encounter, module) and where is that recorded? | Which departmental systems were bought by the department itself? | Who would know if a module you pay for is not in use?
red_flags: The repository lists vendors but not license metrics or quantities. | Modules licensed at implementation have never been reviewed for use.
healthcare_considerations: EHR and ancillary contracts often license modules that were bought during implementation and never switched on; these are candidates for removal at renewal. | Some clinical licenses are tied to regulated workflows or device clearances; involve the department and clinical engineering before changing them.
action_to_2: Add the EHR and the five largest clinical and business applications to the repository (weeks).
action_to_3: Record metric, quantity, renewal date and owner for all applications (one to two months).
action_to_4: Reconcile application licenses annually and link them to the application inventory (months).

question: Are third-party license obligations embedded in vendor systems and medical devices (e.g., bundled Windows or SQL Server) identified?
level_0: Nobody knows which vendor systems or devices include Windows, SQL Server or other embedded software.
level_1: Embedded software is discovered only when a vendor asks for an upgrade or a scan finds it.
level_2: Embedded operating systems and databases are listed for some vendor systems, but license responsibility and update obligations are not stated in contracts.
level_3: Embedded software in vendor systems and medical devices is identified, and contracts state who licenses, patches and supports it.
target_state: Embedded software is tracked with end-of-support dates, MDS2 forms or SBOMs are collected, and obligations are reviewed at each contract renewal.
evidence: List of vendor systems and medical devices with embedded OS or database and license owner — asset inventory or clinical engineering records. | Contract clauses assigning licensing, patching and support responsibility — vendor contracts. | Manufacturer Disclosure Statement for Medical Device Security (MDS2) forms or SBOMs — clinical engineering.
recommended_action: Identify embedded Windows and SQL Server in vendor systems and devices and confirm licensing and patching responsibility in contracts.
probing_questions: Which vendor-supplied servers or appliances run Windows or SQL Server, and who licensed them? | Who is allowed to patch the operating system on imaging modalities, lab analyzers or monitoring servers? | Do you have MDS2 forms or SBOMs for your connected medical devices?
red_flags: Vendor servers run SQL Server editions that appear in no entitlement record. | "The vendor handles it" with no contract clause to show it.
healthcare_considerations: Hospitals cannot patch or relicense regulated medical device software outside manufacturer guidance; rely on manufacturer disclosures, MDS2 forms and SBOMs, and on contract terms. | Biomedical or clinical engineering often owns these devices; the SAM owner needs their inventory, not just IT's.
action_to_2: List vendor systems and devices that run embedded Windows or SQL Server with clinical engineering (weeks).
action_to_3: Confirm in contracts who licenses, patches and supports each embedded component (one to two quarters).
action_to_4: Track end-of-support dates and collect MDS2 forms or SBOMs at each renewal (ongoing).

question: Is actual software deployment discovered automatically across endpoints, servers and cloud?
level_0: Installed software is unknown unless someone checks a machine.
level_1: Manual inventories or one-off scans exist for some servers.
level_2: Endpoint management or EDR reports installed software on most workstations, but servers, vendor-managed systems and cloud workloads are not covered.
level_3: Automated discovery covers endpoints, servers and cloud resources, and results are compared with entitlements at least quarterly.
target_state: Discovery coverage is measured, gaps raise alerts, SaaS use is discovered, and deployment is compared with entitlements at least monthly.
evidence: Software inventory or discovered applications report with device coverage — endpoint management or EDR console. | Server inventory showing OS and SQL Server editions and cores — configuration management tool or hypervisor inventory. | Discovered cloud app report, if licensed — Defender for Cloud Apps or equivalent.
recommended_action: Extend automated software discovery to all endpoints, servers and cloud, measure coverage, and compare deployment with entitlements at least quarterly.
probing_questions: Which tools report installed software, and what percentage of endpoints and servers report in? | How do you see SQL Server editions and core counts on servers? | How do you find SaaS applications that users signed up for themselves? | Which systems are excluded from discovery and why?
red_flags: Coverage is quoted without a device denominator. | Vendor-managed and clinical systems are excluded entirely.
healthcare_considerations: Many clinical devices and vendor appliances cannot take agents; use network-based discovery and vendor attestation for those instead of leaving them out. | Clinicians and departments adopt SaaS tools (scheduling, dictation, patient messaging) that may handle PHI; discovery should feed business associate agreement checks.
action_to_2: Use the existing endpoint management or EDR inventory for all workstations and record coverage (weeks).
action_to_3: Extend discovery to servers and cloud and compare with entitlements quarterly (one to two quarters).
action_to_4: Add SaaS discovery, alert on coverage gaps and compare monthly (months).

question: Is the use of assigned user licenses reviewed at least quarterly?
level_0: License usage is never reviewed; licenses stay assigned until someone complains about cost.
level_1: Unassigned licenses are noticed occasionally in the admin center.
level_2: Usage is reviewed once a year or before a renewal, but inactive and underused accounts are not acted on consistently.
level_3: At least quarterly, unassigned, inactive and underused licenses are identified from usage reports and sign-in data, confirmed with HR or managers, and reassigned or downgraded.
target_state: Review is automated with defined thresholds, results and savings are tracked, and reharvested licenses are reused before new ones are purchased.
evidence: Purchased versus assigned counts per product — Microsoft 365 admin center, Billing > Licenses. | Active users and Microsoft 365 Apps usage reports for 90 or 180 days — Microsoft 365 admin center, Reports > Usage. | Last sign-in export (signInActivity) for licensed accounts — Microsoft Entra admin center or Microsoft Graph. | Record of the last review with actions taken — SAM owner.
recommended_action: Review unassigned, inactive and underused licenses quarterly using usage reports and sign-in data, confirm with HR, then reassign or downgrade.
probing_questions: How many licenses are purchased but unassigned today, per product? | How do you define an inactive user, and how many accounts meet that definition? | Which users have a premium license but use only email or only web apps? | How do you treat per-diem, PRN, agency and on-leave staff in the review?
red_flags: Usage reports show concealed names, so nobody could act on them. | "Inactive" was judged from mailbox logins only.
healthcare_considerations: Per-diem, PRN, agency, locum, resident and student accounts break simple 90- to 180-day inactivity rules; confirm with HR and the medical staff office before removing access or licenses. | Clinicians on shared workstations may use only the EHR and web email; they are candidates for frontline licensing rather than full knowledge-worker plans.
action_to_2: Export purchased, assigned and last-activity data and remove clearly unused licenses (weeks).
action_to_3: Run a quarterly review with defined thresholds and HR confirmation (next quarter).
action_to_4: Automate the review, track savings and reuse reharvested licenses before buying (months).

question: Are the accounts and licenses of departing workforce members removed and reharvested promptly?
level_0: Departed staff accounts stay active and licensed until someone notices.
level_1: IT disables accounts when a manager remembers to tell them; licenses are rarely removed.
level_2: HR notifies IT of employee departures, but contractors, students, agency and vendor accounts are missed and licenses are removed weeks later or not at all.
level_3: Every departure (employee, contractor, student, agency, vendor) triggers account disablement within one business day and license removal per policy, verified by monthly reconciliation with HR and contract lists.
target_state: Disablement is automated from HR and sponsor records, the reconciliation shows no unexplained active accounts, and reharvested licenses are reused.
evidence: Comparison of enabled, licensed accounts with the current HR roster and contractor list — Entra user export and HR report. | Offboarding tickets for the last ten departures with timestamps — service desk. | Accounts with no sign-in for 90 days or more — Microsoft Entra admin center or Microsoft Graph signInActivity.
recommended_action: Disable departing workforce and vendor accounts within one business day, remove licenses per policy, and reconcile monthly against HR records.
hhs_cpg: CPG-E: Revoke Credentials for Departing Workforce Members
probing_questions: How does IT learn that an employee, contractor, student or vendor has left, and how long does it take? | How many enabled, licensed accounts belong to people no longer on the HR roster? | What happens to the mailbox and its license when someone leaves (shared mailbox, retention, license removal)? | Who sponsors vendor and agency accounts and confirms they are still needed?
red_flags: Disabled accounts still hold paid licenses. | Vendor and agency accounts have no named sponsor or end date.
healthcare_considerations: Clinicians often keep EHR, remote access and email accounts after leaving because they may return per diem; require a sponsor and an end date instead of leaving accounts open. | Mailboxes of departed staff may hold PHI and be subject to retention; convert or retain them per policy before removing the license, and confirm retention requirements first.
action_to_2: Reconcile enabled, licensed accounts against the HR roster and disable leavers (days).
action_to_3: Disable within one business day of departure for all workforce types and reconcile monthly (weeks).
action_to_4: Automate disablement from HR and sponsor records and reuse reharvested licenses (months).

question: Are licensing models for shared clinical devices and frontline staff applied correctly?
level_0: Shared workstations use a generic account or a single licensed user for many people.
level_1: Clinical staff receive the same full plan as office staff, or none at all, without analysis.
level_2: Some frontline or device licenses are used, but shared workstation activation, kiosk and device-only scenarios are not reviewed against terms.
level_3: Each workforce group and shared device type is mapped to a licensing model (user, frontline, device-only) and the mapping is checked against current product terms.
target_state: The mapping is reviewed whenever clinical workflows, devices or plans change, and exceptions are approved and documented.
evidence: Mapping of workforce groups and device types to license types — SAM owner. | License assignment counts by plan, including frontline plans — Microsoft 365 admin center. | Device enrollment profile list showing user-affinity and device-only enrollments — Intune admin center.
recommended_action: Map each clinical role and shared device type to the right user, frontline or device-only license and verify against current terms.
probing_questions: How many shared workstations, carts, kiosks and tablets are there, and how do staff sign in to them? | Which clinical roles use desktop Office applications, and which use only the EHR, Teams and web email? | Are any devices enrolled as device-only (kiosk or dedicated), and do they need Conditional Access? | Is shared computer activation enabled for Microsoft 365 Apps on shared workstations?
red_flags: A generic "nurse station" account is licensed and shared by many people. | Frontline licenses assigned to users who need desktop apps on dedicated PCs, or full plans assigned to staff who never use them.
healthcare_considerations: Microsoft describes healthcare clinicians and nursing staff as typical frontline workers; frontline plans can fit staff who work mainly on shared devices, phones or tablets, but confirm app and mailbox needs against the plan comparison and your agreement. | Shared computer activation needs each signed-in user to hold a qualifying license; Intune device-only licenses suit carts and kiosks but do not support Conditional Access or app protection policies.
action_to_2: Inventory shared devices and workforce groups and how each signs in and is licensed (weeks).
action_to_3: Map each group and device type to a licensing model and verify it against current terms (one to two months).
action_to_4: Review the mapping whenever workflows, devices or plans change (ongoing).

question: Does the organization know which security capabilities are already included in its current licenses?
level_0: No one has compared current licenses with the security capabilities they include.
level_1: IT believes some security features are included but cannot list them or their deployment status.
level_2: A list of licensed security capabilities exists, but deployment status is unknown or the list is older than the current plans.
level_3: A current map lists each licensed security capability (identity, endpoint, email, data protection, logging), its deployment status and coverage, verified against current documentation.
target_state: The map is reviewed at each renewal and plan change, gaps are in the security roadmap, and new tool purchases are checked against it first.
evidence: Completed License-Security Map sheet with deployment status — assessment workbook. | Assigned plans and service plans per user — Microsoft 365 admin center or Microsoft Entra licensing view. | Secure Score or equivalent recommendations list — Microsoft Defender portal.
recommended_action: Complete the License-Security Map showing which security capabilities you own, which are deployed, and coverage, verified against current documentation.
hhs_cpg: CPG-E: Multifactor Authentication; CPG-E: Email Security; CPG-E: Strong Encryption
probing_questions: Which Microsoft 365 plans are assigned today, and to how many users each? | For MFA, Conditional Access, endpoint detection and response, email protection and audit logging, which are licensed, which are deployed, and to how many users or devices? | Have you bought a third-party security tool in the last two years that duplicates something already licensed?
red_flags: The map says "included" without saying deployed or not. | A separate tool is paid for a capability already licensed and unused.
healthcare_considerations: Small hospitals often meet several HHS Essential Goals (MFA, email security, encryption) with capabilities they already license; this is usually the fastest, lowest-cost improvement available. | Mixed estates are common (some users on E3, some on Business Premium or frontline plans); map capabilities per plan, not per tenant.
action_to_2: Complete the License-Security Map for the plans you own, marking licensed and deployed (days).
action_to_3: Add coverage per capability and verify statements against current Microsoft documentation (weeks).
action_to_4: Review the map at every renewal and require a map check before new security purchases (ongoing).

question: Are licensed identity protections (multifactor authentication, conditional access) deployed to all users, including clinical and remote access?
level_0: Conditional Access is licensed but no policies exist; MFA is not required.
level_1: Security defaults or per-user MFA cover some administrators or volunteers only.
level_2: Conditional Access requires MFA for most users, but clinical units, vendors or service accounts are excluded without review, or policies are in report-only mode.
level_3: Licensed Conditional Access policies enforce MFA for all users, administrators, vendors and remote access, with documented and approved exclusions and legacy authentication blocked.
target_state: Policies include device compliance and, where licensed, risk-based conditions; phishing-resistant methods are required for administrators; coverage is reported and reviewed.
evidence: Conditional Access policy list with state and exclusions — Microsoft Entra admin center. | Authentication methods registration and usage report — Microsoft Entra admin center. | Sign-in logs filtered for single-factor successful sign-ins over 30 days — Microsoft Entra admin center.
recommended_action: Use licensed Conditional Access to enforce MFA for all users, administrators, vendors and remote access, with documented, approved exclusions only.
probing_questions: Which Conditional Access policies are On, and which are Report-only? | Which groups are excluded from MFA, and who approved each exclusion? | How do clinicians on shared workstations authenticate, and how often are they prompted? | Are risk-based policies licensed for any users, and are they used?
red_flags: Entra ID P1 is licensed through the current plan, yet the tenant relies on per-user MFA or security defaults only. | A large clinical group is excluded "temporarily" with no end date.
healthcare_considerations: Repeated MFA prompts on shared clinical workstations disrupt care; use session-based controls and badge or proximity sign-in at session start rather than excluding whole units. | Vendor remote access to EHR and imaging systems is a recurring gap; vendor accounts need the same MFA policy as staff.
action_to_2: Turn on licensed Conditional Access requiring MFA for administrators, remote access and email (days to weeks).
action_to_3: Remove undocumented exclusions, include vendors, move report-only policies to On and block legacy authentication (weeks).
action_to_4: Add device compliance and, where licensed, risk-based conditions, and report coverage (months).

question: Are licensed endpoint protection and device management deployed to all endpoints, including shared clinical workstations?
level_0: Licensed endpoint management and EDR are not deployed; devices rely on whatever antivirus came installed.
level_1: Licensed tools are deployed to a pilot group or to office PCs only.
level_2: Most corporate workstations are managed and onboarded to EDR, but shared clinical workstations, servers and remote clinics have gaps and no exception list.
level_3: Every supported workstation and server is managed and onboarded to licensed endpoint protection, with exceptions documented and compensating controls applied.
target_state: Coverage is reconciled with the asset inventory at least monthly, unmanaged devices raise alerts, and baselines and EDR settings are reviewed after each change.
evidence: Device inventory with onboarding status — Microsoft Defender portal (Device inventory). | Managed device count and compliance status — Intune admin center. | Exception list with compensating controls — security team.
recommended_action: Onboard every supported workstation and server to licensed device management and EDR, documenting exceptions with compensating controls.
hhs_cpg: CPG-E: Mitigate Known Vulnerabilities; CPG-X: Configuration Management
probing_questions: How many endpoints are in the asset inventory, and how many are managed and onboarded to EDR? | Are shared clinical workstations, carts and kiosks managed the same way as office PCs? | How are servers licensed for endpoint protection (user plans typically do not cover servers)? | Which devices are excluded, and why?
red_flags: EDR coverage is reported without the total device count. | Servers are assumed to be covered by user licenses.
healthcare_considerations: Shared clinical workstations are often left unmanaged to avoid disrupting care; manage them with tested baselines and maintenance windows agreed with nursing leadership. | Vendor-supported and medical device systems may not allow agents; document them as exceptions with segmentation and monitoring, following manufacturer guidance.
action_to_2: Onboard all office and clinical workstations to licensed management and EDR (weeks).
action_to_3: License and onboard servers, document exceptions and apply compensating controls (one to two quarters).
action_to_4: Reconcile coverage with the asset inventory monthly and alert on unmanaged devices (months).

question: Are licensed email protection and data protection features (encryption, data loss prevention, labeling) enabled for PHI?
level_0: Only default email filtering is in place; licensed message encryption and DLP are not configured.
level_1: Users can encrypt email manually if they know how; no DLP policies exist.
level_2: Licensed email protection policies use defaults, and DLP or encryption rules exist in test mode or for one workload only.
level_3: Licensed anti-phishing, attachment and link protection are configured for all mailboxes, and DLP and encryption policies for PHI are enforced on email and file storage.
target_state: Policies are tuned using reports and incidents, sensitivity labels are in use, and coverage and false positives are reviewed at least quarterly.
evidence: Threat policy configuration (anti-phishing, Safe Attachments, Safe Links) — Microsoft Defender portal. | DLP policy list with mode and locations — Microsoft Purview portal. | Message encryption rules — Exchange admin center mail flow rules.
recommended_action: Enable licensed email protection for all mailboxes and enforce PHI data loss prevention and message encryption on email and file storage.
hhs_cpg: CPG-E: Email Security; CPG-E: Strong Encryption
probing_questions: Which email protection policies are on, and do they cover all mailboxes, including shared mailboxes? | How does a clinician send PHI securely to an outside provider or patient? | Which DLP policies exist for PHI, which workloads do they cover, and are they in test or enforce mode? | Which data protection features are licensed for your plans (for example, automatic labeling or endpoint DLP)?
red_flags: DLP policies have been in simulation mode for months. | Shared mailboxes that receive referrals are outside protection policies.
healthcare_considerations: Referral, scheduling and billing mailboxes receive large volumes of external email with attachments and are prime phishing targets; include them explicitly. | Clinicians exchange PHI with outside practices and patients; a usable encryption method reduces workarounds such as personal email or fax-to-email.
action_to_2: Enable licensed anti-phishing, attachment and link protection for all mailboxes (days to weeks).
action_to_3: Enforce PHI DLP and message encryption on email and file storage (one to two months).
action_to_4: Tune policies quarterly and adopt sensitivity labels where licensed (months).

question: Are cloud subscriptions tagged and costs allocated to departments or applications?
level_0: Cloud cost is a single bill; nobody can say which application or department drives it.
level_1: Resources are named inconsistently and a few are tagged.
level_2: A tagging standard exists, but less than most of the spend is tagged and shared costs are not allocated.
level_3: Required tags (owner, application, cost center, environment) are applied to nearly all spend, enforced by policy, and monthly cost is allocated and reviewed by owners.
target_state: Untagged spend is reported and kept near zero, shared costs are split by an agreed method, and owners act on monthly showback.
evidence: Tagging standard — cloud governance documents. | Cost analysis grouped by tag for the last three months — Microsoft Cost Management. | Policy assignments that require or inherit tags — Azure Policy.
recommended_action: Enforce owner, application, cost-center and environment tags by policy and allocate monthly cloud cost to accountable owners.
probing_questions: What share of last month's cloud spend can be attributed to an application or department? | Which tags are mandatory, and how are they enforced? | Who reviews cloud cost each month, and what do they do with it?
red_flags: Tags exist but values are free text with many spellings. | Cost allocation is done once a year in a spreadsheet.
healthcare_considerations: Allocating cost to clinical applications (EHR hosting, imaging archive, interface engine) supports total cost of ownership and modernization decisions. | Grant-funded and affiliated-practice workloads may need separate cost tracking for reporting; tag them from the start.
action_to_2: Define four mandatory tags and apply them to the largest resources (weeks).
action_to_3: Enforce tags with policy and allocate monthly cost to owners (one to two months).
action_to_4: Report untagged spend, allocate shared costs and act on monthly showback (months).

question: Are reservations, savings plans and hybrid-use benefits applied where eligible?
level_0: All cloud resources run at pay-as-you-go rates and existing licenses are not applied.
level_1: Commitment discounts have been discussed but never purchased.
level_2: Some reservations or savings plans exist, but utilization is not monitored and Azure Hybrid Benefit eligibility for Windows Server and SQL Server has not been checked.
level_3: Steady workloads are covered by reservations or savings plans, eligible VMs and databases use Azure Hybrid Benefit, and utilization is reviewed quarterly.
target_state: Commitment coverage and utilization have targets, recommendations are reviewed monthly, and Software Assurance or subscription license eligibility is tracked against hybrid benefit use.
evidence: Reservation and savings plan utilization reports — Azure portal, Reservations and Savings plans. | List of VMs and databases with Azure Hybrid Benefit status — Azure portal or Azure Resource Graph. | Commitment recommendations reviewed — Azure Advisor cost recommendations.
recommended_action: Apply Azure Hybrid Benefit where licenses qualify and cover steady workloads with reservations or savings plans, reviewing utilization quarterly.
probing_questions: Which workloads run around the clock and have been stable for a year? | Do you have reservations or savings plans, and what is their utilization? | Do you own Windows Server or SQL Server licenses with active Software Assurance, and are they applied in Azure? | Who approves a one- or three-year commitment, and how is the risk weighed?
red_flags: Hybrid Benefit is enabled without Software Assurance or qualifying subscription licenses to support it. | Commitments were bought for workloads scheduled to be retired.
healthcare_considerations: Interface engines, EHR integration servers and imaging archives often run continuously and are good commitment candidates once their future is decided. | Savings plan purchases cannot be canceled or refunded; align commitments with the application roadmap before buying.
action_to_2: Check Azure Hybrid Benefit eligibility and apply it where licenses support it (weeks).
action_to_3: Cover steady workloads with reservations or savings plans and review utilization quarterly (one quarter).
action_to_4: Set coverage and utilization targets and review recommendations monthly (months).

question: Are idle or oversized cloud resources identified and rightsized at least monthly?
level_0: Resources are never reviewed after they are created.
level_1: Idle resources are removed occasionally when someone notices a cost spike.
level_2: Cost recommendations are reviewed a few times a year, but unattached disks, idle VMs and oversized resources persist.
level_3: Idle and oversized resources are identified monthly from recommendations and utilization data and rightsized, scheduled or removed with owner approval.
target_state: Detection is automated, non-production resources follow schedules, actions and savings are tracked, and exceptions have owners and review dates.
evidence: Cost recommendations list with status — Azure Advisor. | Utilization data for the top ten VMs by cost — Azure Monitor metrics. | Log of rightsizing actions and savings — cloud owner.
recommended_action: Review cost recommendations monthly, remove idle resources and rightsize oversized ones with owner and vendor approval.
probing_questions: When did you last act on cost recommendations, and what changed? | Are there unattached disks, old snapshots or test VMs left from projects or migrations? | Are non-production systems shut down outside working hours?
red_flags: Recommendations are dismissed in bulk without reasons. | Migration leftovers (old disks, snapshots) are older than six months.
healthcare_considerations: Clinical systems may be sized to vendor specifications; rightsize only with the vendor's agreement and test performance during peak clinical hours. | Downtime and disaster recovery environments can look idle; confirm their role in recovery plans before removing them.
action_to_2: Remove unattached disks, old snapshots and abandoned test resources (days).
action_to_3: Review recommendations monthly and rightsize or schedule with owner approval (one quarter).
action_to_4: Automate detection and schedules and track savings and exceptions (months).

question: Are budgets and spending alerts configured for cloud subscriptions?
level_0: No budgets or alerts exist; overspending is discovered on the invoice.
level_1: A single budget exists at the billing account level with alerts to one person.
level_2: Budgets exist for some subscriptions, but alerts go to people who do not own the resources and are not acted on.
level_3: Every subscription or resource group has a budget with alerts routed to its owner and finance, and alerts are acknowledged.
target_state: Anomaly detection is used, alerts trigger documented investigation, and budgets are revised from forecasts at least quarterly.
evidence: Budget list with thresholds and recipients — Microsoft Cost Management, Budgets. | Last three alert notifications and actions taken — cloud owner.
recommended_action: Configure budgets and alerts for every subscription, routed to resource owners and finance, and investigate every alert.
probing_questions: Which subscriptions have budgets, and who receives the alerts? | What happened the last time an alert fired? | Would you notice a sudden doubling of daily spend within a week?
red_flags: Alerts go to a shared mailbox nobody reads. | Budgets were set once and never revised.
healthcare_considerations: Imaging archives and log collection can grow quickly with volume; budget alerts catch growth before it lands on the invoice. | With small IT teams, route alerts to both the technical owner and finance so an absence does not leave spend unwatched.
action_to_2: Create a budget with alerts for each subscription (days).
action_to_3: Route alerts to owners and finance and record actions taken (weeks).
action_to_4: Add anomaly alerts and revise budgets quarterly from forecasts (months).

question: Has eligibility for nonprofit, healthcare or rural hospital licensing programs and discounts been verified?
level_0: No one has checked whether the organization qualifies for any program or discount.
level_1: Someone has heard of a program but eligibility has not been checked.
level_2: Eligibility has been checked for one program, but the result was not applied or documented.
level_3: Eligibility for applicable programs (for example, nonprofit offers and the Microsoft program for rural hospitals announced in 2024) has been verified, documented and applied where eligible.
target_state: Program eligibility and terms are rechecked before each renewal, end dates of promotional terms are in the renewal calendar, and benefits are tracked.
evidence: Eligibility check records and correspondence — SAM owner or reseller. | Applied program pricing or offers on invoices — accounts payable. | End dates of promotional terms in the renewal calendar — contract register.
recommended_action: Verify eligibility for nonprofit and rural hospital programs, apply what qualifies, and record promotional term end dates in the renewal calendar.
probing_questions: Is the organization a nonprofit, government-owned, critical access or rural emergency hospital, and is it independent or part of a system? | Have you applied for or been offered any Microsoft program for rural hospitals or nonprofits, and what was the outcome? | When do any promotional or no-cost terms end, and what happens to pricing then?
red_flags: A no-cost offer was accepted with no plan for the price at term end. | Eligibility was assumed from another hospital's experience.
healthcare_considerations: Microsoft announced a cybersecurity program for rural hospitals in June 2024 that described nonprofit pricing (up to 75% discount) for independent critical access and rural emergency hospitals and a one-year no-cost security offer for other rural hospitals; confirm current terms and availability before planning on it. | Hospitals that are part of a health system may be covered by the system's agreement rather than individual programs; check with the parent organization.
action_to_2: Check eligibility for nonprofit and rural hospital programs with your reseller or Microsoft (weeks).
action_to_3: Apply eligible programs, document the result and record term end dates (one quarter).
action_to_4: Recheck eligibility and terms before every renewal and track benefits (ongoing).

question: Is the agreement type (e.g., Enterprise Agreement, CSP, MCA) reviewed against current size and needs before renewal?
level_0: The organization does not know which agreement type it buys under.
level_1: The agreement type is known, but renewals continue on the same type and plan mix by default.
level_2: Alternatives were discussed with a reseller at the last renewal, but without usage data, term options or a documented comparison.
level_3: Before each renewal, agreement type, term length, billing frequency and plan mix are compared with current headcount, usage and needs, and the decision is documented.
target_state: The comparison uses reconciled usage and multi-year forecasts, includes flexibility terms (for example, cancellation windows and reduction rights), and outcomes are reviewed after renewal.
evidence: Agreement and enrollment documents with term dates — contract register. | Subscription terms, billing frequency and renewal settings — Microsoft 365 admin center or reseller portal. | Documented comparison of agreement and plan options from the last renewal — procurement files.
recommended_action: Before each renewal, compare agreement type, term length, reduction rights and plan mix against current usage and documented needs.
probing_questions: Do you buy through an Enterprise Agreement, a CSP partner, a Microsoft Customer Agreement directly, or a mix? | What are your term lengths, and when can you reduce quantities without penalty? | How has headcount changed since the last renewal, and is it expected to change? | Who compared alternatives at the last renewal, and where is the comparison?
red_flags: Annual subscriptions were bought for a seasonal or shrinking workforce without considering flexibility. | The only comparison was a single reseller quote.
healthcare_considerations: Microsoft describes the Enterprise Agreement as designed for organizations with at least 500 users or devices; many small hospitals buy through CSP partners instead, where cancellation is typically limited to the first days of a term. | Affiliations and mergers can change the right agreement quickly; review agreement fit when ownership or management changes.
action_to_2: Document current agreement type, terms, billing and reduction rights (weeks).
action_to_3: Compare agreement and plan options against usage and needs before the next renewal (next renewal cycle).
action_to_4: Use reconciled usage and forecasts and review outcomes after each renewal (ongoing).

question: Are savings from license optimization reinvested in documented security or modernization priorities?
level_0: Savings are not identified or are absorbed into the general budget unnoticed.
level_1: Savings are mentioned informally but not quantified.
level_2: Savings are quantified but returned to the general budget without a decision on reinvestment.
level_3: Savings are tracked from invoices and reinvested through documented leadership decisions in security or modernization priorities.
target_state: A standing rule allocates realized savings to the security and modernization roadmap, and outcomes of reinvestment are reported.
evidence: Savings log based on invoice changes — SAM owner. | Leadership decision or budget record allocating savings — finance or steering minutes.
recommended_action: Track realized licensing savings from invoices and reinvest them through documented decisions in security and modernization priorities.
probing_questions: How much did license optimization save last year, measured from invoices? | Who decided what happened to those savings? | Which security gaps from this assessment could be funded by reharvested or downgraded licenses?
red_flags: Savings are projected from list prices and never confirmed on invoices. | Reinvestment is promised but no budget line exists.
healthcare_considerations: Linking reharvested license spend to an HHS Essential Goal gap (for example, MFA coverage or email security) gives a hospital board a concrete, budget-neutral improvement. | Savings on annual terms are realized only at renewal; plan reinvestment timing accordingly.
action_to_2: Quantify last year's licensing savings from invoices (weeks).
action_to_3: Present savings to leadership with a proposed reinvestment in documented priorities (next budget cycle).
action_to_4: Adopt a standing reinvestment rule and report outcomes (months).

question: Is license compliance risk assessed with a defensible effective license position?
level_0: Compliance position is unknown; under- or over-licensing would be discovered only in an audit.
level_1: The team believes it is compliant but has no calculation.
level_2: An effective license position exists for Microsoft 365 user subscriptions, but not for server, SQL Server, virtualization or clinical application licensing.
level_3: An effective license position for major vendors compares entitlements with deployment and usage rules, and gaps are remediated or accepted by leadership.
target_state: The position is refreshed at least annually and before each renewal or true-up, assumptions are documented, and audit requests follow a defined response process.
evidence: Effective license position workbook for Microsoft and the top clinical vendors — SAM owner. | Deployment data for servers and databases (editions, cores, hosts) — discovery tool or hypervisor inventory. | Audit response procedure — SAM or compliance documentation.
recommended_action: Maintain an effective license position for Microsoft and major clinical vendors, including server and SQL Server, refreshed before renewals and true-ups.
probing_questions: How many SQL Server and Windows Server cores are deployed, and how are they licensed, including virtualization? | Have you received a vendor audit or license review request in the last three years, and how was it handled? | Who reviews licensing terms when infrastructure changes (new hosts, cloud migration, disaster recovery sites)?
red_flags: The position counts installations but ignores licensing rules for virtualization and disaster recovery. | The position was prepared by the vendor or reseller and never checked internally.
healthcare_considerations: Disaster recovery and downtime environments for clinical systems often run duplicate SQL Server and Windows Server instances; confirm whether your licensing terms cover them. | Treat any under-licensing finding as a risk to confirm with a licensing specialist before taking action or disclosing it.
action_to_2: Calculate an effective license position for Microsoft 365 and Windows Server and SQL Server (weeks to one quarter).
action_to_3: Extend the position to the top clinical vendors and remediate or accept gaps (one to two quarters).
action_to_4: Refresh the position annually and before renewals and define an audit response process (ongoing).

question: Is there a complete inventory of applications with business owner, technical owner, vendor and hosting model?
level_0: No application list exists, or the only list is a software purchase ledger or an EHR module list kept by one analyst.
level_1: A spreadsheet lists the major clinical and financial systems, but owners, hosting model and departmental or vendor-hosted tools are missing or out of date.
level_2: Most applications are listed with a technical owner and vendor; business owners, hosting model or PHI handling are blank for many rows, and departmental or SaaS tools are incomplete.
level_3: Every application, including departmental, SaaS and vendor-hosted systems, has a named business owner, technical owner, vendor, hosting model, user group and PHI flag, reconciled against discovery data and contracts.
target_state: The inventory is reconciled automatically against endpoint and server discovery, single sign-on applications and accounts payable at least quarterly, and unregistered applications raise a ticket.
evidence: Application inventory with owner, vendor, hosting and PHI columns completed — App Portfolio Triage sheet or the configuration management database export. | Reconciliation record comparing the inventory to software discovery, single sign-on application list and accounts payable vendors — IT asset management or finance. | Sample of five applications picked by the assessor from the accounts payable vendor list, traced to inventory rows.
recommended_action: Inventory every application, including departmental and vendor-hosted systems, with business owner, technical owner, vendor, hosting and PHI flag.
probing_questions: Show me the list. How many rows, and when was it last changed? Who changes it? | Which applications did a department buy directly on a credit card or through a clinical budget, such as a dictation or a scheduling tool? | If the laboratory system went down tonight, who is the business owner who decides on downtime procedures, and is that person on the list? | How do you reconcile the list with what discovery tools, single sign-on and accounts payable show? | Which applications run on medical devices or on vendor-managed servers in your building?
red_flags: The inventory was built for a past EHR conversion or audit and has not been touched since. | Business owner is recorded as IT for clinical applications.
healthcare_considerations: Departmental systems (cardiology, pharmacy, dietary, wound care, imaging viewers) are often bought outside IT and run on unmanaged servers; they are the rows most often missing. | Vendor-hosted EHR and revenue cycle systems still belong in the inventory: you remain responsible for access, interfaces, downtime procedures and the business associate agreement.
action_to_2: Fill the App Portfolio Triage sheet from contracts, accounts payable and discovery data for all known applications (one to two weeks).
action_to_3: Assign a business and technical owner to every row and reconcile against discovery and single sign-on lists (one to two months).
action_to_4: Automate quarterly reconciliation against discovery, single sign-on and accounts payable and ticket every unregistered application (months).

question: Are dependencies between applications (interfaces, databases, HL7 or FHIR feeds, shared infrastructure) documented?
level_0: Dependencies are not documented; interface knowledge sits with the interface analyst or the vendor.
level_1: The interface engine shows active channels, but nobody has mapped them to source and destination applications, databases or shared servers.
level_2: An interface list exists for the EHR and laboratory, but file transfers, database links, shared servers and vendor-hosted connections are missing.
level_3: An interface catalog covers every HL7 v2, FHIR, file, database and API connection with source, destination, message type, owner and transport, and critical applications have a dependency map including shared infrastructure.
target_state: The catalog is reconciled against the interface engine and firewall rules after every change, and it is used to assess impact in every change request and outage review.
evidence: Interface catalog with source, destination, message type, transport and owner — interface team or integration vendor. | Active channel list exported from the interface engine, compared with the catalog by the assessor. | Dependency map for the three most critical applications showing servers, databases, storage, identity and network dependencies.
recommended_action: Catalog every interface, including those outside the interface engine, and map dependencies for critical applications first.
probing_questions: If we shut down this database server for maintenance, which applications and interfaces stop? How do you know? | How many active channels does the interface engine show, and how many are in your catalog? | Which interfaces bypass the engine: point-to-point feeds, nightly file drops, direct database reads, vendor VPN tunnels? | Who is alerted when an ADT, orders or results feed stops, and how long before someone notices?
red_flags: The catalog lists only interfaces that pass through the engine. | Nobody can say which applications share a database server or a file share.
healthcare_considerations: ADT, orders and results feeds (HL7 v2 ADT, ORM, ORU messages) drive patient safety: a silent results interface means clinicians do not see laboratory values. Treat interface failure as a clinical risk, not only a technical one. | Interfaces to reference laboratories, state immunization and public health registries and health information exchanges often run on vendor-managed tunnels or file transfers that IT did not build and does not monitor.
action_to_2: Export the interface engine channel list and document every critical clinical feed with source, destination and owner (two to four weeks).
action_to_3: Add non-engine connections and shared infrastructure and map dependencies for every critical application (one to three months).
action_to_4: Reconcile the catalog with the engine and firewall rules after each change and require impact analysis from it (ongoing).

question: Is each application classified by its criticality to patient care, revenue cycle and operations?
level_0: No criticality rating exists; everything is treated as equally important, or IT decides informally during an outage.
level_1: IT has an informal view of the top systems (EHR, laboratory, pharmacy), not written down or agreed with clinical leaders.
level_2: A criticality rating exists for some applications but was set by IT alone, or it is not used for recovery order or investment.
level_3: Every application has a documented criticality rating with defined criteria, approved by clinical and business owners, and the rating drives recovery order and recovery objectives.
target_state: Ratings are reviewed annually and after major incidents, tied to recovery objectives and the risk analysis, and used in budget and modernization prioritization.
evidence: Applications and data criticality analysis with criteria and ratings — contingency plan or business impact analysis. | Approval record from clinical and business leadership (meeting minutes or signed document). | Recovery order list that matches the criticality ratings — disaster recovery plan.
recommended_action: Rate every application's criticality with clinical and business owners and use the rating to set recovery order.
probing_questions: What are the criteria for critical? Who signed off on them, and is there a clinical leader on that list? | In a ransomware event, in what order would you restore systems, and where is that written? | Which applications were rated critical only because a department asked loudly? | When was the applications and data criticality analysis last updated for the contingency plan?
red_flags: Every application is rated critical. | The restore order in the disaster recovery plan contradicts the criticality ratings.
healthcare_considerations: Criticality must consider dependencies: the EHR may be critical, but so is the identity service, the interface engine and the printing service it relies on. | Rate by patient care impact first (medication administration, results, imaging, blood bank), then revenue cycle and operations; clinical leaders, not IT, should approve the patient care ratings.
action_to_2: Define a three-to-five level criticality scale and rate the top 20 applications with clinical input (two to four weeks).
action_to_3: Rate every application, obtain clinical and business approval and align the recovery order (one to two months).
action_to_4: Review ratings annually and after major incidents and link them to recovery objectives and budget decisions (ongoing).

question: Is the application inventory reviewed at least annually and updated with every change?
level_0: The inventory is never updated after it is created.
level_1: The inventory is updated when someone remembers, usually before an audit or a budget cycle.
level_2: New applications are usually added, but retirements, owner changes and hosting changes are not captured, and there is no scheduled review.
level_3: Change management requires an inventory update for new, changed and retired applications, and a full review with owners is completed at least annually.
target_state: Inventory completeness is measured (for example rows with missing owners) and reported, and procurement and contract processes cannot complete without an inventory entry.
evidence: Change records referencing inventory updates — change management system. | Date and attendance of the last full inventory review — meeting minutes. | Procurement or contract checklist that includes IT review and inventory registration.
recommended_action: Make inventory updates mandatory in change management and purchasing, and review the full inventory with owners annually.
probing_questions: Show me the last three applications added and the last one retired. Are they reflected? | Does the change form have a field that forces an inventory update? | Can purchasing buy software or sign a SaaS contract without IT being told?
red_flags: Retired applications are still listed with active owners, or decommissioned servers still appear.
healthcare_considerations: Clinical departments frequently sign SaaS agreements directly; tying inventory registration to contract and business associate agreement review catches them.
action_to_2: Add an inventory update step to the change form and the purchasing checklist (days).
action_to_3: Run a full annual review with every business owner and record the date (one to two months per cycle).
action_to_4: Report inventory completeness quarterly and block procurement of unregistered software (months).

question: Do you know which applications depend on platforms past end of support (e.g., Windows 10, older Windows Server or SQL Server)?
level_0: Platform versions are not tracked; nobody can say which applications run on unsupported operating systems or databases.
level_1: IT knows of some old servers but has no list linking platforms to applications.
level_2: Operating system versions are known from discovery, but database, middleware and framework versions, embedded systems and vendor-managed servers are not linked to applications.
level_3: Every application row records its operating system, database and key runtime versions with support end dates from the vendor's lifecycle page, and unsupported dependencies are reported to leadership.
target_state: Support end dates are tracked automatically from discovery data, platforms approaching end of support are flagged at least 18 months ahead, and the list feeds the roadmap and budget.
evidence: Platform support status report linking each application to operating system and database versions — discovery tool or CMDB export. | Lifecycle dates for each platform from the vendor's official lifecycle page (for Microsoft, learn.microsoft.com lifecycle). | List of devices excluded from discovery (vendor-managed, medical device workstations) with the reason.
recommended_action: Link every application to its operating system and database versions and official support end dates, including vendor-managed systems.
probing_questions: How many Windows 10 devices remain, and which clinical applications or devices require them? | Which applications still run on Windows Server 2012 R2 or earlier, or on SQL Server 2016 or earlier? Who confirmed it? | Which vendor-managed servers and medical device workstations are excluded from your discovery data? | Which platforms reach end of support in the next 18 months, for example Windows Server 2016?
red_flags: The report covers servers but not databases or desktops attached to clinical equipment. | Extended Security Updates are assumed to be purchased but nobody can show the enrollment.
healthcare_considerations: Many clinical vendors certify their software only on specific operating system and database versions; an unsupported platform may be a vendor certification problem, not only an IT upgrade. | Workstations attached to imaging, laboratory analyzers or other regulated devices may run old Windows versions under manufacturer control; track them separately and ask the manufacturer for its supported configuration.
action_to_2: Export operating system and database versions from discovery and map them to applications in the triage sheet (two to three weeks).
action_to_3: Add vendor-managed and device-attached systems, record official support end dates and report to leadership (one to two months).
action_to_4: Automate end-of-support flagging 18 months ahead and feed it into roadmap and budget planning (months).

question: Is there a funded plan for each unsupported platform (upgrade, isolate, retire or purchase extended updates)?
level_0: No plan exists for unsupported platforms.
level_1: IT has an intention to upgrade, but no owner, date or funding.
level_2: Plans exist for some platforms, such as the Windows 10 refresh, but others lack owners or funding, or rely on Extended Security Updates without an exit date.
level_3: Each unsupported platform has an approved plan (upgrade, isolate, retire or extended updates as a bridge) with an owner, a target date and approved funding, tracked to closure.
target_state: Plans are reviewed monthly with leadership, risk acceptance is signed for every residual exception, and budget is reserved before platforms reach end of support.
evidence: Remediation plan per unsupported platform with owner, decision and date — project tracker or risk register. | Approved budget line or purchase order — finance. | Signed risk acceptance for each exception — risk register.
recommended_action: Approve a funded plan with owner and date for each unsupported platform; use Extended Security Updates only as a bridge.
probing_questions: For each unsupported platform on the list, what is the decision, who owns it and when is it done? | Is the money in this year's budget, or is it a request? | If you bought Extended Security Updates, what is the exit plan before they end? | Who signed the risk acceptance for the systems you will not fix this year?
red_flags: Extended Security Updates are treated as the plan instead of a bridge. | The plan waits on a vendor upgrade that has no committed date.
healthcare_considerations: Clinical vendor upgrades often require a new version of the application, interface retesting and clinical validation; budget for vendor services and clinical informatics time, not only licenses and hardware. | Where the manufacturer controls the device, the plan is often isolation plus a request for the manufacturer's supported configuration and patch guidance, not a direct upgrade.
action_to_2: Record a decision, owner and target date for every unsupported platform (two to four weeks).
action_to_3: Obtain funding approval, sign risk acceptance for exceptions and track each plan to closure (one quarter).
action_to_4: Review plans monthly with leadership and reserve budget before platforms reach end of support (ongoing).

question: Are vendor support status, roadmap and contract terms tracked for clinical applications?
level_0: Vendor support status and contract terms are not tracked; renewals arrive as surprises.
level_1: Contracts are filed in procurement, but nobody tracks support end dates, version support or vendor roadmap.
level_2: A vendor list exists with renewal dates, but supported versions, end-of-life notices and security obligations are not recorded.
level_3: A vendor register records, for each clinical application, the supported version, support end date, roadmap commitments, renewal date and security and incident notification terms, and it is reviewed before each renewal.
target_state: Vendor reviews are scheduled at least annually and before renewals, use the register to negotiate upgrade and security terms, and vendor end-of-life notices trigger roadmap updates.
evidence: Vendor register with supported version, support end date, renewal date and security terms — procurement or IT. | Vendor end-of-life or support notices received in the last two years. | Minutes or notes from the last vendor review before a renewal.
recommended_action: Track supported version, support end date, roadmap and security terms for each clinical vendor and review before renewals.
probing_questions: Which version of your laboratory or pharmacy system are you on, and until when does the vendor support it? | Which vendors have announced end of life for a product you use? | Do contracts specify which operating system and database versions the vendor will certify, and when? | When is the next renewal, and what will you ask the vendor for?
red_flags: The register has renewal dates but no supported-version information.
healthcare_considerations: Small hospitals often run versions several releases behind because upgrades require vendor services they cannot schedule; ask whether you are on a version the vendor still patches. | Clinical vendors may require specific operating system and database versions; negotiate certification timelines for supported platforms in renewals.
action_to_2: Build a vendor register for clinical applications with versions, support end dates and renewals (two to four weeks).
action_to_3: Add roadmap and security terms and review the register before every renewal (one quarter).
action_to_4: Hold annual vendor reviews and use the register to negotiate upgrade and certification commitments (ongoing).

question: Are legacy systems that cannot be upgraded (including medical device software) isolated with compensating controls?
level_0: Legacy and device systems sit on the same flat network as user workstations and servers.
level_1: Some legacy systems are on a separate VLAN, but traffic between segments is not filtered.
level_2: Legacy systems are segmented with some filtering, but rules are broad, vendor remote access is unrestricted, or there is no exception register.
level_3: Each non-upgradable system is in a restricted segment allowing only documented flows, has brokered vendor access, monitoring and an exception record with owner, compensating controls and review date.
target_state: Allowed flows are verified at least quarterly against observed traffic, anomalies alert the monitoring team, and each exception has a replacement plan reviewed by leadership.
evidence: Segmentation design and firewall or access control rule set for legacy and device segments — network team. | Exception register with owner, compensating controls and review date — risk register. | Manufacturer Disclosure Statement for Medical Device Security (MDS2) or manufacturer guidance for device systems — clinical engineering.
recommended_action: Isolate non-upgradable systems in restricted segments allowing only documented flows, with brokered vendor access and recorded exceptions.
references: NIST CSF 2.0 PR.IR; CISA ZTMM v2.0 Networks
probing_questions: Pick one legacy system. What can talk to it, and what can it talk to? Show me the rule. | Can a user workstation reach a device workstation over remote desktop or file sharing? | How does the manufacturer or vendor connect for support, and who approves each session? | Is there an exception record for each system, and when was it last reviewed?
red_flags: Segments exist but allow any traffic between them. | Vendor access to legacy systems uses permanent always-on connections.
healthcare_considerations: Hospitals cannot patch regulated device software outside the manufacturer's guidance; isolation, monitoring and manufacturer-supplied patches are the usual controls. Involve clinical engineering, which often owns these devices. | Imaging modalities and laboratory analyzers need specific flows (for example DICOM to the image archive, results to the laboratory system); document and allow only those.
action_to_2: Move non-upgradable systems into dedicated segments and block user-to-device traffic (weeks to months).
action_to_3: Restrict to documented flows, broker vendor access and record each exception with compensating controls (one to two quarters).
action_to_4: Verify flows against observed traffic quarterly, alert on anomalies and track replacement plans (ongoing).

question: Does each application have a documented disposition (retire, retain, rehost, replatform, refactor, replace or isolate)?
level_0: No dispositions exist; applications stay until they break or a vendor forces a change.
level_1: IT leaders have opinions about which systems should go, but nothing is documented.
level_2: Dispositions are recorded for some applications, typically those in a current project, without consistent criteria or owner approval.
level_3: Every application has a disposition from the kit's list, based on documented criteria (risk, value, criticality, cost), approved by the business and clinical owner.
target_state: Dispositions are revisited at least annually and on triggering events (vendor end of life, contract renewal, incident), and outcomes are tracked against the roadmap.
evidence: Disposition and Final decision columns completed in the App Portfolio Triage sheet. | Approval record from application and clinical owners — governance minutes. | Written disposition criteria.
recommended_action: Record an owner-approved disposition for every application using documented criteria and the App Portfolio Triage sheet.
probing_questions: For your ten most expensive applications, what is the decision and who approved it? | What criteria did you use, and are they written down? | Which applications are marked Retain only because nobody looked at them?
red_flags: All applications are marked Retain. | The suggested disposition from the workbook was copied as the final decision without owner review.
healthcare_considerations: Retiring a clinical system requires a plan for legally retained records: archive in a viewable form or keep a read-only instance; do not decommission until medical records and compliance agree. | Replace decisions for EHR-adjacent systems often depend on what the EHR vendor offers natively; check before buying another point solution.
