action_to_2: Use the triage sheet to propose dispositions for the top 20 applications by priority (two weeks).
action_to_3: Write disposition criteria and obtain owner approval for every application (one to two months).
action_to_4: Review dispositions annually and on vendor end-of-life notices, renewals and incidents (ongoing).

question: Is there a sequenced modernization roadmap aligned with business priorities and regulatory deadlines?
level_0: No roadmap exists; projects start in response to failures, vendor deadlines or audits.
level_1: A list of desired projects exists, without sequence, dependencies, owners or funding.
level_2: A roadmap covers the next year's major projects but is not linked to dispositions, dependencies or platform end-of-support dates.
level_3: A funded roadmap sequences work in waves by risk, value and dependencies, reflects known end-of-support dates and tracks regulatory developments, and is approved by leadership.
target_state: The roadmap is reviewed quarterly against progress and risk, re-sequenced when dates or risks change, and reports benefits achieved.
evidence: Modernization roadmap with waves, owners, dates and funding status. | Leadership approval record — board or executive committee minutes. | Last quarterly progress review.
recommended_action: Build a funded roadmap in waves from approved dispositions, sequenced by risk, value, dependencies and platform end-of-support dates.
probing_questions: What will be done in the next two quarters, and why in that order? | Which items are funded and which are requests? | Does the roadmap show dependencies, for example the database upgrade that must precede the application upgrade? | How do platform end dates, such as Windows Server 2016 in January 2027, appear in the plan?
red_flags: The roadmap is the EHR vendor's upgrade calendar and nothing else. | Regulatory items cite a proposed rule as if it had a fixed compliance date.
healthcare_considerations: The HIPAA Security Rule update published as a proposed rule in January 2025 is still proposed; track it as a development, not a deadline, and plan around controls you already need. | Schedule waves around clinical calendars (EHR upgrades, regulatory surveys, census peaks) and around the small number of analysts who know each system.
action_to_2: Turn approved dispositions into a one-year list of projects with owners (two to four weeks).
action_to_3: Sequence the work in waves by risk, value and dependencies, add end-of-support dates and obtain funding approval (one quarter).
action_to_4: Review the roadmap quarterly, re-sequence on new risks and report benefits (ongoing).

question: Are redundant applications with overlapping functions identified for consolidation?
level_0: Overlaps are not identified.
level_1: IT knows anecdotally that several tools do the same job, but nothing is documented.
level_2: Some overlaps are documented, for example two document management systems, but no capability map or decisions exist.
level_3: A capability-to-application map exposes overlaps, and each overlap has a consolidation decision with an owner.
target_state: New purchases are checked against the capability map before approval, and consolidation savings are tracked.
evidence: Capability-to-application map — App Portfolio Triage sheet Business function column or a separate map. | Consolidation decisions with owners — governance minutes.
recommended_action: Map business capabilities to applications, decide on each overlap and check new purchases against the map.
probing_questions: How many tools do you have for document scanning, faxing, secure messaging and dictation? | Does the EHR already include a module that duplicates a departmental tool? | Is a new purchase checked against what you already own?
red_flags: Consolidation is blocked because no one owns the decision across departments.
healthcare_considerations: Mergers, affiliations and physician practice acquisitions bring duplicate scheduling, billing and document systems; consolidation reduces interfaces and attack surface. | Native EHR modules may replace point solutions, but confirm workflow fit with clinical users before deciding.
action_to_2: Group applications by business function in the triage sheet to expose obvious overlaps (one to two weeks).
action_to_3: Build a capability map and record a consolidation decision and owner for each overlap (one to two months).
action_to_4: Check every new purchase against the map and track consolidation savings (ongoing).

question: Is the total cost of ownership known for major applications?
level_0: Application costs are unknown beyond the license invoice.
level_1: License and maintenance fees are known for some applications.
level_2: License and maintenance costs are known for major applications, but infrastructure, interfaces, support staff and vendor services are not.
level_3: For each major application, licensing, maintenance, infrastructure or hosting, interfaces, vendor services and internal staff time are estimated with a documented method.
target_state: Total cost of ownership is updated annually, used in disposition decisions and business cases, and compared to alternatives before renewals.
evidence: Cost per application with method — finance or IT, Annual cost column of the triage sheet. | Business case or renewal analysis that used total cost of ownership.
recommended_action: Estimate total cost of ownership, including infrastructure, interfaces and staff time, for the top applications by spend.
probing_questions: For your laboratory system, what does it cost in total each year: license, maintenance, servers, interfaces, people? | Where do infrastructure and hosting costs get allocated? | Have you ever compared the cost of keeping an application to the cost of replacing it?
red_flags: Cost equals the maintenance invoice only.
healthcare_considerations: Interface costs (engine licenses, per-interface vendor fees, analyst time) and after-hours vendor support are often the hidden part of clinical application cost.
action_to_2: Record license and maintenance cost for the top 20 applications by spend (two weeks).
action_to_3: Add infrastructure, interfaces, services and staff time with a documented method (one to two months).
action_to_4: Update annually and use total cost of ownership in every disposition and renewal decision (ongoing).

question: Are changes deployed through a controlled, repeatable release process with approval and rollback?
level_0: Changes are made directly in production by whoever has access, without records.
level_1: Changes are announced by email or chat, but approval, testing and rollback depend on the individual.
level_2: A change process exists for major systems, but emergency and vendor changes bypass it, rollback plans are not written, or configurations are not baselined.
level_3: All production changes, including vendor-performed changes, follow an approved process with risk rating, test evidence, scheduled window, written rollback plan and configuration baseline.
target_state: Change success, failure and rollback rates are measured, rollback is rehearsed for high-risk changes, and deployments of in-house code are automated and repeatable.
evidence: Change records for a sample of recent changes with approval, test evidence and rollback plan — change management system. | Release procedure document. | Configuration baseline for a critical application or server.
recommended_action: Route every production change, including vendor changes, through approval with test evidence, a scheduled window and written rollback plan.
probing_questions: Show me the last three changes to a clinical system. Where are the approval, test evidence and rollback plan? | When the vendor applies an upgrade or patch remotely, does it go through your change process? | How many emergency changes last quarter, and were they reviewed afterwards? | When was a rollback last performed, and did it work?
red_flags: Vendor changes are excluded from the process. | Rollback plans say restore from backup without a tested time estimate.
healthcare_considerations: In 24x7 operations, change windows must be agreed with nursing, pharmacy and laboratory leadership and paired with downtime procedures; a failed overnight change can affect medication administration and results. | Many clinical vendors perform upgrades remotely; require that their work follows your change approval, communication and verification steps.
action_to_2: Require a change record with approval and rollback plan for every change to critical applications (weeks).
action_to_3: Extend the process to vendor and emergency changes and baseline configurations (one quarter).
action_to_4: Measure change outcomes, rehearse rollback for high-risk changes and automate in-house deployments (months).

question: Is automated testing used for critical applications before release?
level_0: No testing is done before release, or testing is done by users in production.
level_1: Testing is manual and informal, done by an analyst or super-user without scripts.
level_2: Manual test scripts exist for some clinical workflows, but they are not run on every release and nothing is automated.
level_3: Critical workflows have documented regression tests run on every release, with automated tests for in-house code and interfaces where practical, and results are retained.
target_state: Automated regression covers critical workflows and interfaces, runs in the release pipeline, and failures block release; test coverage is reviewed after incidents.
evidence: Test scripts and results for the last two releases of a critical application — release records. | Description of the test environment and test data source (synthetic or de-identified). | Automated test reports from a pipeline, where in-house code exists.
recommended_action: Script regression tests for critical clinical workflows and interfaces, run them every release and automate where practical.
probing_questions: When the vendor delivers an upgrade, what do you test, who tests it and where are the results? | Do you have a test environment with representative, de-identified or synthetic data? | Which interfaces are tested automatically, for example sending test HL7 messages and checking the result? | Has an upgrade ever broken a workflow that testing should have caught?
red_flags: Testing uses copies of production data containing PHI in an uncontrolled environment.
healthcare_considerations: Clinical validation (order to result, medication order to administration, admission to billing) should be scripted with clinical informatics and run on every upgrade; vendor testing does not cover your configuration. | Small hospitals often lack a full test environment; at minimum validate interfaces with test patients agreed with the vendor.
action_to_2: Write regression scripts for the top clinical workflows and interfaces with clinical informatics (weeks).
action_to_3: Run them on every release, retain results and automate tests for in-house code and interfaces (one to two quarters).
action_to_4: Integrate automated regression in the release pipeline so failures block release (months).

question: Are secure development practices (code review, dependency scanning, secrets management) applied to in-house and customized code?
level_0: In-house scripts, reports and integrations are written without review, version control or scanning.
level_1: Some code is in version control, but review and scanning are optional and secrets are embedded in scripts or configuration files.
level_2: Version control and peer review are used for main projects, but dependency scanning and secrets management are missing or inconsistent, and interface scripts are excluded.
level_3: All in-house and customized code is in protected version control with mandatory review, dependency and vulnerability scanning and secrets in a managed vault; vendors provide secure development attestations.
target_state: Scanning gates releases, vulnerabilities are tracked to closure with timelines, software bills of materials are kept for in-house software, and practices are reviewed against the SSDF annually.
evidence: Repository settings showing branch protection and required review — source control platform. | Dependency and secret scanning results for the last month. | Vendor secure development attestation or questionnaire responses — procurement.
recommended_action: Put all in-house code in reviewed version control, scan dependencies and secrets, and request secure development evidence from vendors.
references: NIST SP 800-218 PO.1, PS.1, PW.4, PW.7, RV.1
probing_questions: What code do you own: interface scripts, reports, integrations, web forms, scheduled jobs? Where is it stored? | How are database and interface credentials stored in scripts? | Who reviews a change before it reaches production? | What do you ask vendors about their secure development practices?
red_flags: Interface or report scripts live on a server share outside version control. | Service account passwords appear in scripts.
healthcare_considerations: Small hospitals' custom code is usually interface transformations, report queries and integration scripts; these touch PHI and need the same controls as applications. | Ask clinical vendors for secure development evidence; the CISA secure software self-attestation form is one example of what producers provide to federal agencies.
action_to_2: Move all in-house code into version control with required review and remove secrets from scripts (weeks).
action_to_3: Add dependency and secret scanning, a managed vault and vendor attestation requests (one quarter).
action_to_4: Gate releases on scanning, track vulnerabilities to closure and keep software bills of materials (months).

question: If AI-assisted engineering is used, is it governed by policy (approved tools, data restrictions, human review)?
level_0: AI tools are used for code or configuration without any policy, or IT does not know whether they are used.
level_1: Leaders informally discourage pasting sensitive data into AI tools, but there is no written policy or approved tool list.
level_2: A draft or general AI policy exists, but approved engineering tools, PHI prohibitions and review requirements are not defined or enforced.
level_3: A policy names approved AI tools under appropriate agreements, prohibits PHI and secrets in prompts and test data, and requires human review of every AI-generated change before release.
target_state: Use of approved tools is logged, review compliance is checked in change records, unapproved tools are blocked, and the policy is reviewed at least annually.
evidence: AI-assisted engineering policy with approved tools — policy library. | Change records showing human review of AI-assisted changes. | Agreements for approved AI tools covering data handling (business associate agreement where PHI could be involved).
recommended_action: Publish an AI-assisted engineering policy with approved tools, no PHI or secrets in prompts, and mandatory human review.
references: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.PO; NIST SP 800-218 PO.3
probing_questions: Who uses AI tools to write scripts, queries or configuration today, and which tools? | What stops someone from pasting an HL7 message with patient data into a public tool? | How do you know an AI-generated change was reviewed by a person before release?
red_flags: The policy exists but nobody can list the approved tools.
healthcare_considerations: Interface messages, error logs and report outputs often contain PHI; the policy must cover these artifacts, not only patient records. | Use synthetic test data for AI-assisted interface or report development.
action_to_2: Publish a short policy naming approved tools and prohibiting PHI and secrets in prompts (weeks).
action_to_3: Require and record human review of AI-assisted changes in change management (one quarter).
action_to_4: Log use, block unapproved tools and review the policy annually (months).

question: Are backups of critical applications and data protected from tampering and is restoration tested?
level_0: Backups are not taken for some critical systems, or nobody knows whether they work.
level_1: Backups run, but they are reachable with the same administrator credentials as production and restoration is not tested.
level_2: Backups exist for critical systems and some file restores are tested, but backups are not immutable or offline, or full application restores have never been tested.
level_3: Backups of critical applications are immutable or offline, protected by separate credentials and MFA, and a full application restore is tested at least annually with results documented.
target_state: Restores of every critical application are tested on a schedule against recovery objectives, backup integrity is monitored, and failures alert the team.
evidence: Backup configuration showing immutability or offline copy and separate credentials — backup console. | Restoration test report for a critical application with duration and issues — IT. | Vendor backup and restore commitments for hosted systems — contract or service description.
recommended_action: Make backups immutable or offline with separate credentials, and test full restores of critical applications at least annually.
references: HIPAA 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(A),(D); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.DS, RC.RP
probing_questions: If an attacker obtained domain administrator rights, could they delete or encrypt your backups? | When did you last restore a complete critical application, not a file, and how long did it take? | Do vendor-hosted systems back up your data, and have you seen a restore test? | Are interface engine configurations and database backups included?
red_flags: Restore testing means restoring a single file. | Backup console uses domain administrator accounts.
healthcare_considerations: Restoring a clinical system includes its interfaces, interface engine configuration, identity dependencies and print queues; test the whole chain, not only the database. | For vendor-hosted EHRs, confirm what the vendor restores, how fast, and how you access data during their outage (read-only copy or downtime reports).
action_to_2: Back up every critical application and test one full restore (weeks).
action_to_3: Make backups immutable or offline with separate credentials and test full restores annually (one quarter).
action_to_4: Schedule restore tests for every critical application against recovery objectives and monitor integrity (months).

question: Do critical applications have recovery time and recovery point objectives that are tested?
level_0: No recovery objectives are defined.
level_1: IT has informal expectations of how fast systems come back, not agreed with owners.
level_2: Recovery objectives are written for some applications but were never tested, or tests showed gaps that remain open.
level_3: Every critical application has recovery time and point objectives approved by its owner, and recovery exercises confirm they are achievable or document approved gaps.
target_state: Recovery exercises run on a schedule, results are reported to leadership, and gaps are funded and closed; objectives are reviewed when criticality changes.
evidence: Recovery objectives per critical application approved by owners — disaster recovery plan. | Disaster recovery test report with achieved times — IT. | Vendor recovery commitments for hosted systems — contract.
recommended_action: Agree recovery time and point objectives with owners for each critical application and prove them in recovery exercises.
probing_questions: For the laboratory system, how long can the hospital operate without it, and how much data can it lose? | When was recovery last tested, and what time did you actually achieve? | Do vendor contracts for hosted systems state recovery commitments matching your objectives? | What happens if several critical systems must be recovered at once?
red_flags: Objectives were set by IT without clinical owners. | Tests recover one system in isolation, never the dependency chain.
healthcare_considerations: Objectives must match how long downtime procedures can safely carry operations; clinical leaders should confirm that paper workflows can last that long. | In a ransomware scenario, multiple systems are lost at once; test recovery of the identity service, interface engine and EHR connectivity together.
action_to_2: Agree recovery objectives for critical applications with clinical and business owners (weeks).
action_to_3: Run recovery exercises, document achieved times and record approved gaps (one to two quarters).
action_to_4: Schedule exercises, report results to leadership and fund gap closure (ongoing).

question: Are downtime procedures for clinical workflows documented and exercised?
level_0: No documented downtime procedures exist.
level_1: Downtime binders exist in some units but are outdated, and staff are unsure how to use them.
level_2: Procedures are documented for major clinical areas, but they are not exercised, downtime forms or reports are stale, or recovery back-entry is not defined.
level_3: Every clinical department has current downtime procedures, including forms, read-only access or reports and back-entry steps, and exercises them at least annually.
target_state: Downtime exercises include extended multi-day scenarios, results drive improvements, and downtime report devices and read-only copies are checked on a schedule.
evidence: Downtime procedures per department with last revision date — clinical policy library. | Exercise records and after-action reports — clinical informatics or emergency management. | Check log for downtime report devices or read-only copies — IT.
recommended_action: Document downtime procedures with read-only access and back-entry steps for every clinical department, and exercise them annually.
probing_questions: If the EHR is down for three days, how do nurses see medication administration records and allergies? | Where are downtime reports printed or stored, and when were they last checked? | When did each unit last run a downtime exercise, and what went wrong? | How are paper records entered back after recovery, and who reconciles them?
red_flags: Procedures assume the downtime lasts hours, not days. | Downtime report devices have not been checked since they were installed.
healthcare_considerations: Ransomware outages can last weeks; procedures should cover extended downtime, including laboratory, pharmacy, imaging, registration and diversion decisions. | Downtime report workstations and read-only copies are themselves systems that must be patched, isolated and tested.
action_to_2: Update downtime procedures for the top clinical departments and check downtime report devices (weeks).
action_to_3: Cover every department, including back-entry, and exercise each at least annually (one to two quarters).
action_to_4: Run extended multi-day scenarios and feed results into procedures and recovery planning (ongoing).

question: Is monitoring in place to detect application outages and performance degradation?
level_0: Outages are discovered when clinicians call the help desk.
level_1: Basic server up/down checks exist for some servers; applications and interfaces are not monitored.
level_2: Servers and some applications are monitored, but interface queues, response times and vendor-hosted systems are not, or alerts go to an unattended mailbox.
level_3: Critical applications are monitored end to end, including availability, response time and interface queues, with alerts routed to an accountable on-call team at all hours.
target_state: Synthetic transactions test key clinical workflows, alert thresholds are tuned from incident reviews, and availability is reported to owners.
evidence: Monitoring dashboard showing critical applications and interfaces — monitoring tool. | Alert routing and on-call schedule. | Last three outages with detection source (alert or user report) — incident records.
recommended_action: Monitor critical applications and interface queues end to end with alerts routed to on-call staff at all hours.
probing_questions: How did you find out about the last outage: an alert or a phone call? | If the results interface queue stops processing at 2 a.m., who is alerted and how quickly? | Who receives alerts outside business hours? | How do you know a vendor-hosted system is slow before users complain?
red_flags: Alerts go to a shared mailbox nobody watches at night.
healthcare_considerations: Interface queue depth is often the first sign of a clinical outage; monitor queues and message age, not only whether the engine service is running. | Small teams rely on one on-call person; route alerts so a single missed page does not leave a results feed down until morning.
action_to_2: Monitor availability of critical applications and interface engine queues with alerts to on-call staff (weeks).
action_to_3: Add response time and vendor-hosted systems and route alerts to accountable teams at all hours (one quarter).
action_to_4: Add synthetic clinical transactions and tune thresholds from incident reviews (months).

question: Is there a cloud foundation (identity, network, security, cost governance) in place before migrations?
level_0: Cloud resources are created ad hoc, or migrations are planned without a foundation.
level_1: A cloud subscription exists with a few workloads, created by one person without standard policies.
level_2: Some foundation elements exist (for example identity integration) but network design, security policies, logging or cost controls are incomplete.
level_3: A documented foundation provides identity integration, network segmentation and connectivity, security baselines, logging, backup, tagging and budgets, and every migration lands on it.
target_state: The foundation is deployed as code, policy compliance is monitored continuously, and drift is corrected automatically or ticketed.
evidence: Cloud foundation design and policy assignments — cloud management console. | Policy compliance report for existing subscriptions. | Tagging and budget configuration — cost management console.
recommended_action: Establish a governed cloud foundation for identity, network, security, logging and cost before migrating any workload.
references: Microsoft Cloud Adoption Framework (Ready); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.PS
probing_questions: Before the next workload moves, where will it land, and who designed that environment? | How are administrator access, network connectivity to the hospital and logging handled in the cloud? | Are policies enforced, for example blocking public storage or untagged resources? | Does the cloud provider agreement include a business associate agreement?
red_flags: Workloads with PHI run in a subscription created for a pilot.
healthcare_considerations: Clinical applications moved to cloud still need low-latency, resilient connectivity to on-premises devices and interfaces; design for loss of the internet link, including downtime procedures. | Small teams benefit from a standard, small foundation (one landing zone pattern) rather than a large enterprise design they cannot operate.
action_to_2: Document current cloud subscriptions and apply identity, logging and budget basics (weeks).
action_to_3: Establish a documented foundation with network, security baselines, backup and tagging before further migrations (one quarter).
action_to_4: Deploy the foundation as code and monitor policy compliance continuously (months).

question: Are business associate agreements in place with all cloud and SaaS providers that handle PHI?
level_0: Business associate agreements are not tracked for cloud and SaaS providers.
level_1: Agreements exist for the EHR vendor and a few others, but nobody knows which other providers handle PHI.
level_2: A list of agreements exists, but it is not reconciled with the application inventory, or security requirements are not reviewed.
level_3: Every provider that creates, receives, maintains or transmits PHI has a signed business associate agreement linked to its inventory row, and a security review is completed before onboarding.
target_state: Agreements and security reviews are tracked with renewal dates, reviewed periodically and on incidents, and onboarding cannot proceed without them.
evidence: Business associate agreement register linked to the application inventory — compliance or legal. | Vendor security reviews for PHI-handling providers — IT or security. | Onboarding checklist requiring agreement and review.
recommended_action: Confirm a signed business associate agreement and a security review for every provider that handles PHI.
probing_questions: Which providers in your inventory handle PHI, and does each have a signed agreement? | What about transcription, fax, messaging, patient engagement and analytics tools bought by departments? | What security questions do you ask before signing, and who reviews the answers?
red_flags: The agreement register is held by compliance and has never been compared with the application inventory.
healthcare_considerations: Departmental SaaS tools (scheduling, patient messaging, transcription) are the usual gap; reconcile the agreement register with the full inventory. | A business associate agreement does not replace a security review; include incident notification and recovery commitments in contracts.
action_to_2: Flag PHI-handling providers in the inventory and confirm a signed agreement for each (weeks).
action_to_3: Link agreements to inventory rows and complete security reviews before onboarding (one quarter).
action_to_4: Track agreements and reviews with renewal dates and block onboarding without them (ongoing).

question: Are interfaces moving toward standards-based APIs (e.g., HL7 FHIR) where applicable?
level_0: Interfaces are point-to-point custom formats or file drops, and standards are not considered.
level_1: HL7 v2 is used for core feeds, but new interfaces are still built as custom files or direct database access.
level_2: Standards are preferred informally, but there is no interface standard, API inventory or security requirement for APIs.
level_3: A documented interface standard prefers HL7 v2 or FHIR APIs over custom formats for new and modernized interfaces, and APIs are inventoried, authenticated and logged.
target_state: Interface choices are reviewed against the standard in design review, legacy custom interfaces have replacement plans, and API usage and errors are monitored.
evidence: Interface standard or design guideline — integration team. | Interface catalog showing interface type per connection. | API inventory with authentication method and logging.
recommended_action: Adopt an interface standard preferring HL7 v2 or FHIR, and inventory, authenticate and log every API.
probing_questions: How was the last new interface built, and why that way? | Which applications read the EHR database directly? | Which FHIR APIs are exposed, who can call them and how is access logged?
red_flags: FHIR endpoints are exposed by vendors but not in the inventory or security review.
healthcare_considerations: HL7 v2 will remain the backbone for ADT, orders and results for years; FHIR is typically added for new uses (patient access, apps, data exchange). Modernize where it reduces custom code, not for its own sake. | Direct database reads from the EHR break on upgrades and bypass audit; replace them with supported interfaces or APIs.
action_to_2: Write a short interface standard preferring HL7 or FHIR and record interface type in the catalog (weeks).
action_to_3: Inventory, authenticate and log every API and apply the standard to new interfaces (one to two quarters).
action_to_4: Plan replacement of custom and direct-database interfaces and monitor API usage (months).

question: Are data classification, retention and migration rules for PHI defined before applications are moved?
level_0: No classification or retention rules exist for application data.
level_1: Retention is decided case by case when a system is retired or moved.
level_2: A retention schedule exists for medical records, but application data classification and migration rules (what moves, what is archived, what is destroyed) are not defined.
level_3: PHI classification, retention periods and migration rules are documented and approved by compliance and records management, and applied in every migration and retirement plan.
target_state: Compliance with the rules is verified after each migration, legacy archives are inventoried, and destruction is recorded.
evidence: Data classification and retention policy — compliance or records management. | Migration or retirement plan applying the rules for a recent project. | Destruction or archive records — records management.
recommended_action: Define PHI classification, retention and migration rules with records management before moving or retiring any application.
probing_questions: When you retire the old system, where will its records live, and for how long? | Who decides what data moves to the new system and what is archived? | How do you verify that copies and test environments are deleted after migration?
red_flags: Old servers are kept running indefinitely because nobody decided on retention.
healthcare_considerations: Retention periods for medical records vary by state and record type; records management and counsel decide, not IT. | Legacy systems kept only for record lookup are often unpatched; a read-only archive with access controls reduces the risk.
action_to_2: Document retention requirements with records management for applications in the next migration (weeks).
action_to_3: Approve classification, retention and migration rules and apply them in every migration and retirement plan (one quarter).
action_to_4: Verify compliance after each migration and inventory legacy archives (ongoing).

question: Is multifactor authentication enforced for remote access, email and privileged accounts?
level_0: No MFA, or MFA only for a few volunteers.
level_1: MFA on some remote access (for example the VPN) but not on email or administrator accounts.
level_2: MFA on remote access and email for most users; exceptions are undocumented; administrators use SMS or voice; vendor accounts are excluded.
level_3: MFA is enforced (not report-only) for all remote access, email, administrators and third-party/vendor access; exceptions are documented, approved and reviewed.
target_state: Phishing-resistant methods (FIDO2 security keys, Windows Hello for Business or certificate-based authentication) are required for administrators and remote access; legacy authentication is blocked; coverage is monitored and gaps raise alerts.
evidence: Conditional Access (or equivalent) policy list showing each policy's state is On, not Report-only — identity provider admin portal. | Authentication methods registration and usage report — identity provider reporting. | Sign-in logs filtered for successful single-factor sign-ins over the last 30 days — identity provider sign-in logs. | Inventory of remote entry points with the MFA status of each — remote access or network team.
recommended_action: Enforce MFA on all remote access, email, vendor and administrator accounts; move administrators to phishing-resistant methods.
references: HIPAA 45 CFR 164.312(d); CISA ZTMM v2.0 Identity; NIST CSF 2.0 PR.AA
probing_questions: List every remote entry point (VPN, VDI/Citrix, vendor portals, RDP gateways, EHR remote access). Is MFA enforced on each one? | How do vendors connect for support, and who owns those accounts? | Are any access policies in report-only or audit mode? Is legacy authentication blocked? | How many accounts are excluded from MFA, why, and who approves exclusions? | How are emergency (break-glass) accounts protected and monitored?
red_flags: "We have MFA" but the policy is in report-only mode or excludes a large group. | Vendor or service accounts are excluded from MFA without compensating controls. | The VPN has MFA but a second, older entry point (RDP gateway, legacy portal) does not.
healthcare_considerations: Shared clinical workstations: MFA at every login disrupts care, so teams exempt whole units. Use badge-tap or proximity sign-in with MFA at session start instead of blanket exemptions. | Vendor remote access is a recurring gap; in 2024 congressional testimony, UnitedHealth Group's CEO acknowledged that the Change Healthcare server attackers entered through did not have MFA.
action_to_2: Enforce MFA on all remote access, email and vendor accounts first (days to weeks).
action_to_3: Remove undocumented exclusions, turn report-only policies on and block legacy authentication (weeks).
action_to_4: Require phishing-resistant methods for administrators and remote access and alert on coverage gaps (months).

question: Does every workforce member use unique credentials, including on shared clinical workstations?
level_0: Generic logins (for example a unit or station account) are the normal way clinicians sign in to workstations and clinical applications.
level_1: Most staff have personal accounts, but several units, nursing stations or device workstations still run under shared logins that nobody inventories.
level_2: Shared accounts are inventoried and reduced, but some remain on clinical workstations, kiosks or vendor systems without an owner or compensating controls.
level_3: Every person signs in with a unique account; remaining non-person accounts (kiosks, device service accounts) are inventoried, owned, restricted to one function and reviewed at least annually.
target_state: Shared workstations use fast user switching or badge-based sign-in with per-user sessions; the directory is scanned automatically for new generic or shared accounts and any found raise an alert.
evidence: Directory export of accounts without a linked person or HR record, with owner and purpose — directory or identity governance report. | EHR or clinical application user list showing generic or departmental logins — application security administrator. | Configuration of the shared-workstation sign-in method (fast user switching, badge tap) — endpoint management console.
recommended_action: Inventory and retire shared logins; give shared clinical workstations fast, badge-based personal sign-in so unique accounts stay practical.
probing_questions: Walk me through how a nurse signs in at a nursing station at shift change. Whose name appears in the EHR audit trail? | Which accounts in the directory are not tied to a person (unit, station, scanner, kiosk, vendor)? Who owns each? | Do any medical device workstations or departmental systems (lab, imaging, pharmacy) use a single shared login? | If a generic account were misused tonight, how would you tell who used it?
red_flags: Account names such as unit, station, nurse or scan with recent interactive sign-ins. | The answer covers the EHR but not departmental systems or device workstations.
healthcare_considerations: Generic logins exist because sign-in takes too long at the bedside; removing them without a fast sign-in option (badge tap, session roaming) pushes staff back to workarounds. | Some vendor-managed modalities and analyzers ship with a single operator account; record them as exceptions with the vendor and clinical engineering, and restrict them by network segment.
action_to_2: Inventory every shared and generic account with an owner and purpose (two to four weeks).
action_to_3: Replace shared logins on clinical workstations with personal accounts and document the remaining non-person accounts (one to three months).
action_to_4: Deploy badge-based fast user switching and automated detection of new shared accounts (three to six months).

question: Are administrator accounts separate from daily user accounts and granted only when needed?
level_0: IT staff use their everyday accounts, which also read email and browse the web, for administration.
level_1: Some administrators have separate admin accounts, but daily accounts still hold domain or cloud administrator rights.
level_2: Separate admin accounts exist for all IT staff, but they hold standing high privilege, are not reviewed and are sometimes used to read email or browse.
level_3: Separate admin accounts are used only for administration, are protected by MFA, privileged groups are reviewed at least quarterly and service accounts are inventoried.
target_state: Highest privileges are granted just in time with approval and expiry, administrative work happens from dedicated admin workstations, and privileged activity is logged and alerted.
evidence: Membership of privileged directory and cloud roles with last-review date — directory and cloud identity admin portals. | Privileged identity or access management activation log for the last 90 days — PIM/PAM console. | Local administrator password management configuration and coverage — endpoint management console.
recommended_action: Separate administrator accounts from daily accounts, review privileged groups quarterly and move top privileges to just-in-time elevation.
hhs_cpg: CPG-E: Separate User and Privileged Accounts
references: CISA ZTMM v2.0 Identity; NIST CSF 2.0 PR.AA
probing_questions: How many people are in your top-level directory and cloud administrator roles today? When did someone last remove a member? | Do your administrators' daily accounts have any administrative rights anywhere, including local administrator on workstations? | Where do administrators perform admin tasks from, and can that device read email or browse? | Which service accounts have domain-level rights, and do EHR or vendor installers require them? | How are local administrator passwords on workstations and servers managed?
red_flags: Admin accounts exist but sign-in logs show them used for email or web. | Vendor or integration service accounts are members of domain administrator groups. | The same local administrator password is used on all workstations.
healthcare_considerations: EHR, interface engine and imaging vendors often request domain administrator rights for installs or support; grant time-bound, scoped rights and remove them afterward. | In a small IT team, two or three people hold all admin rights and cover each other 24x7; design break-glass accounts so an outage at 2 a.m. does not force standing privilege.
action_to_2: Create separate admin accounts for every administrator and remove admin rights from daily accounts (two to four weeks).
action_to_3: Review privileged groups quarterly, require MFA on admin accounts and rotate unique local administrator passwords (one to three months).
action_to_4: Adopt just-in-time elevation with approval and dedicated admin workstations (three to six months).

question: Are the accounts of departing workforce members and vendors revoked promptly?
level_0: Accounts are disabled only when someone remembers; former staff and vendors remain active.
level_1: HR emails IT about departures and IT disables directory accounts, but application, remote access and vendor accounts are missed.
level_2: A documented offboarding checklist covers the directory and main applications, but timing varies, contractors and vendors are not always included and nobody reconciles.
level_3: Access for employees, contractors, students, volunteers and vendors is revoked within a defined timeframe (for example 24 hours) across directory, EHR and remote access, verified by monthly reconciliation.
target_state: Revocation is triggered automatically from HR and vendor-contract records, covers connected applications, and reconciliation exceptions are tracked to closure.
evidence: Sample of recent terminations compared with account disable dates across directory, EHR and remote access — HR report and system audit logs. | Monthly reconciliation report of active accounts against HR and contractor rosters — identity or IT operations team. | List of enabled accounts with no sign-in in 90 days — directory report.
recommended_action: Revoke access for all departing staff, contractors and vendors within a defined timeframe, with expiry dates and monthly reconciliation.
hhs_cpg: CPG-E: Revoke Credentials for Departing Workforce Members
probing_questions: Pick three people who left last month. Show me when each account was disabled in the directory, the EHR and remote access. | How do you learn that a travel nurse, locum, student or vendor engineer has finished? | Which applications have their own user stores outside single sign-on? | How are accounts handled for staff who leave involuntarily?
red_flags: Revocation evidence covers only employees, not contractors, agency staff or vendors. | Many enabled accounts have not signed in for months.
healthcare_considerations: Hospitals rely on agency nurses, locum physicians, students and affiliated physicians who are not on HR payroll; sponsor-based expiry dates are needed for these populations. | Medical staff with privileges at several facilities may keep remote EHR access long after they stop practicing; include medical staff office records in reconciliation.
action_to_2: Document an offboarding checklist covering directory, EHR, remote access and vendor accounts (two weeks).
action_to_3: Set a revocation timeframe, add expiry dates for non-employees and reconcile monthly (one to two months).
action_to_4: Automate revocation from HR and contract records across connected applications (three to six months).

question: Is there a complete inventory of endpoints, servers and connected medical devices?
level_0: No inventory, or only purchase records and spreadsheets that do not match what is on the network.
level_1: IT has a spreadsheet of workstations and servers; clinical engineering keeps a separate list of medical equipment without network details.
level_2: Endpoint and server inventory comes from management tools, but connected medical and building devices are partly listed and the lists are not reconciled.
level_3: One inventory covers endpoints, servers, network gear and connected medical devices with owner, location, operating system, support status and network segment, reconciled with discovery at least quarterly.
target_state: Passive and active discovery keeps the inventory current automatically, unknown devices raise alerts, and medical devices are linked to MDS2 forms, SBOMs and manufacturer patch guidance.
evidence: Inventory export with coverage metrics (discovered versus recorded devices) — CMDB, endpoint management or asset discovery tool. | Clinical engineering medical equipment list cross-referenced to network data — biomedical/clinical engineering system. | File of MDS2 forms and SBOMs for connected medical devices — clinical engineering or procurement.
recommended_action: Build one inventory of endpoints, servers and connected medical devices with owners, support status and segment, reconciled with network discovery.
references: CISA ZTMM v2.0 Devices; NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM
probing_questions: How many networked devices are there in total, and how was that number produced? | Who owns the infusion pumps, imaging modalities, lab analyzers and patient monitors, and are they in the same inventory as IT assets? | When a new device shows up on the network, how do you learn about it? | For each medical device, do you know the operating system, whether it is supported and which segment it is on?
red_flags: IT and clinical engineering totals differ widely and nobody can explain the gap. | The inventory has no operating system or support status for medical devices.
healthcare_considerations: Medical devices often cannot take endpoint agents; passive network discovery is the practical way to find them without disrupting patient care. | Clinical engineering, not IT, usually owns medical devices; the inventory only works if both teams agree on one record and one owner per device.
action_to_2: Merge IT and clinical engineering lists into one inventory with owners (one to two months).
action_to_3: Add discovery, operating system, support status and segment, and reconcile quarterly (two to four months).
action_to_4: Automate discovery with alerts for unknown devices and link MDS2 and SBOM data (six months or more).

question: Are known exploited vulnerabilities remediated within defined, risk-based timeframes?
level_0: No regular vulnerability scanning; patching happens when a system breaks or a vendor calls.
level_1: Workstations receive automatic operating system updates, but servers, network devices and third-party software are patched irregularly and nothing is scanned.
level_2: Scanning runs and patching follows a monthly cycle, but there are no written timeframes, internet-facing systems are not prioritized and exceptions are not recorded.
level_3: Written remediation timeframes by severity exist, with known exploited vulnerabilities (CISA KEV) and internet-facing systems first; exceptions are approved, compensated and tracked.
target_state: Remediation performance against timeframes is measured and reported monthly, KEV matches are flagged automatically from scan data, and unpatchable assets have documented compensating controls.
evidence: Vulnerability scan report for internet-facing and internal systems with age by severity — scanner console or CISA Vulnerability Scanning report. | Written vulnerability management standard with timeframes — policy library. | Exception register with compensating controls and expiry dates — security or risk team.
recommended_action: Scan internet-facing systems, patch CISA KEV findings first and enforce written remediation timeframes with tracked exceptions.
references: CISA ZTMM v2.0 Devices; NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA, PR.PS
probing_questions: Show me the scan of internet-facing systems from the last 30 days. Which findings are on the CISA KEV catalog and how old are they? | What are your written remediation timeframes, and how often do you meet them? | How are firewalls, VPN appliances and remote access gateways patched, and who watches their advisories? | What happens when a vendor forbids patching a system that runs the EHR interface or a medical device?
red_flags: Patching is described only for Windows workstations. | Edge devices (firewall, VPN, file transfer) are patched less often than desktops. | Exceptions have no expiry date or compensating control.
healthcare_considerations: Medical devices and some clinical systems may only be patched per manufacturer guidance; record the manufacturer position and compensate with segmentation and monitoring rather than ignoring the finding. | Patch windows compete with 24x7 clinical operations; agree standing maintenance windows with nursing and the EHR team so urgent KEV fixes do not wait for the next quarterly downtime.
action_to_2: Scan internet-facing systems and patch KEV-listed findings first; CISA offers free external scanning (weeks).
action_to_3: Publish remediation timeframes by severity with an approved exception register (one to two months).
action_to_4: Measure and report remediation against timeframes monthly with automatic KEV flagging (three to six months).

question: Is device health and compliance checked before access to PHI is granted?
level_0: Any device with valid credentials, including personal computers and phones, can reach email, the EHR and file shares.
level_1: Hospital-owned devices are managed, but there is no check at sign-in; personal devices reach PHI freely.
level_2: Compliance policies exist for some device types, but access policies do not require compliance or are in report-only mode.
level_3: Access to email, cloud storage and remote EHR access requires a managed, compliant device or an approved protected app; non-compliant devices are blocked or limited.
target_state: Device risk signals (encryption, patch level, EDR status) are evaluated continuously and access is adjusted automatically, with exceptions reviewed.
evidence: Access policies that require compliant or managed devices, showing enforcement state — identity provider admin portal. | Device compliance report with counts of non-compliant devices — endpoint management console. | Sign-in log sample showing access from unmanaged devices — identity provider sign-in logs.
recommended_action: Require a managed, compliant device or protected app for email, cloud storage and remote EHR access.
references: CISA ZTMM v2.0 Devices; NIST CSF 2.0 PR.AA
probing_questions: Can I read hospital email or open the EHR remote portal from my personal laptop today? | What makes a device compliant, and how many managed devices are non-compliant right now? | How do physicians who are not employees access PHI from their own devices? | Are compliance-based access policies enforced or in report-only mode?
red_flags: Compliance policies are defined but no access policy uses them. | Affiliated physicians are excluded from device requirements without an alternative.
healthcare_considerations: Affiliated and community physicians use their own devices; app protection policies or a virtual desktop are usually more practical than full enrollment. | Shared clinical workstations and devices on carts must stay compliant without user action; schedule updates around shifts so compliance checks do not lock clinicians out mid-care.
action_to_2: Define compliance policies for each managed device type (weeks).
action_to_3: Enforce compliant-device or protected-app requirements for email, cloud storage and remote EHR access (one to three months).
action_to_4: Feed EDR and patch signals into access decisions and review exceptions (three to six months).

question: Are secure configuration baselines applied and configuration drift monitored?
level_0: Devices are configured individually by whoever builds them; there is no standard.
level_1: A standard workstation image exists, but servers and network devices are configured by hand and settings change over time.
level_2: Baselines exist for workstations and some servers, but they are not applied to all devices and drift is not checked.
level_3: Approved baselines cover workstations, servers and network devices, are applied through management tools, and drift is reported at least monthly.
target_state: Baseline compliance is measured continuously, drift is corrected automatically where safe, and deviations are approved exceptions with owners.
evidence: Baseline documents or policy profiles with version and approval date — endpoint management or group policy. | Baseline compliance report by device type — endpoint management console. | Network device configuration backups and change records — network team.
recommended_action: Apply approved security baselines to workstations, servers and network devices through management tools and report drift monthly.
references: CISA ZTMM v2.0 Devices; NIST CSF 2.0 PR.PS
probing_questions: What security baseline do you apply to workstations and servers, and when was it last reviewed? | What percentage of devices currently comply with the baseline, and how do you know? | How are firewalls, switches and wireless controllers configured and backed up? | How do you handle vendor-built servers that cannot take the baseline?
red_flags: The baseline is the default image and has never been reviewed. | Vendor servers are excluded from baselines without a list.
healthcare_considerations: EHR, PACS and interface engine vendors often specify server settings; document vendor-required deviations as approved exceptions rather than excluding the servers entirely. | Clinical workstations need kiosk-style lockdown (no local admin, restricted USB) balanced against peripherals such as label printers, scanners and signature pads.
action_to_2: Adopt a published security baseline for workstations and servers (weeks).
action_to_3: Apply baselines through management tools to all device types and report drift monthly (two to four months).
action_to_4: Monitor compliance continuously and auto-remediate drift with approved exceptions (six months).

question: Is the network segmented so that medical devices, clinical systems, guest and corporate traffic are separated?
level_0: A flat network: workstations, servers, medical devices and building systems share the same network.
level_1: Guest wireless is separated, but medical devices, servers and user workstations share segments.
level_2: Separate segments exist for some medical devices or servers, but traffic between them is largely allowed and rules are not reviewed.
level_3: Medical devices, clinical servers, user workstations, building systems and guests are in separate segments, and traffic between segments is allowed only by documented rules reviewed at least annually.
target_state: Medical device segments are restricted to the specific flows each device needs, rule changes go through review, and unexpected traffic between segments raises alerts.
evidence: Segmentation design listing segments and permitted flows (without addresses) — network team. | Firewall rule review record with date and reviewer — network or security team. | Count of medical devices by segment from the inventory — asset inventory.
recommended_action: Separate medical devices, clinical servers, users, building systems and guests into segments with documented, reviewed rules between them.
references: CISA ZTMM v2.0 Networks; NIST CSF 2.0 PR.IR
probing_questions: Can a workstation in registration reach an infusion pump or imaging modality directly? | How are medical devices assigned to segments when clinical engineering installs them? | Which rules between segments allow any service or any destination, and who approved them? | Where do backup systems and their management interfaces sit?
red_flags: Segments exist but the rule between them allows any traffic. | Segmentation is described only for guest wireless.
healthcare_considerations: Many medical devices run unsupported operating systems that the manufacturer will not let you patch; segmentation is the main compensating control and should follow the communication needs in the MDS2 form. | Clinical engineering and the device vendor must take part in rule design; blocking a needed flow can stop results reaching the EHR or stop a modality sending images.
action_to_2: Move medical devices and building systems off user networks into their own segments (one to three months).
action_to_3: Restrict traffic between segments to documented rules and review them annually (three to six months).
action_to_4: Restrict medical device segments to required flows and alert on unexpected traffic (six to twelve months).

question: Is remote and vendor access brokered through controlled, logged and time-limited connections?
level_0: Vendors connect with always-on VPN accounts, remote desktop exposed to the internet or remote control tools installed ad hoc.
level_1: Most vendors use the VPN with shared or permanent accounts; nobody has a complete list of vendor connections.
level_2: Vendor connections are listed and use named accounts with MFA, but access is always on and sessions are not logged.
level_3: Vendor and remote administrative access goes through a broker or gateway with MFA, named accounts, access only to specific systems, approval or schedule-based enablement, and session logs.
target_state: Vendor sessions are just in time, recorded and reviewed, unapproved remote access tools are detected and blocked, and each connection is tied to a contract and owner.
evidence: Inventory of vendor remote access paths with method, account, MFA status and owner — remote access or network team. | Session logs or recordings from the access broker for the last 30 days — remote access broker console. | Endpoint report of installed remote access tools — EDR or software inventory.
recommended_action: Route all vendor access through an MFA-protected broker with named accounts, system-specific, time-limited sessions and session logs.
references: CISA ZTMM v2.0 Networks; NIST CSF 2.0 PR.AA
probing_questions: List every vendor that can connect remotely. How does each one connect, and is access on when nobody has asked for it? | Are any remote control tools installed by vendors on servers or medical device workstations? | Can a vendor reach anything beyond the system it supports once connected? | If a vendor's credentials were stolen tonight, what would stop someone using them?
red_flags: Vendor accounts are shared by the vendor's support team. | Remote access tools appear on servers that are not on the vendor list.
healthcare_considerations: EHR, PACS, lab and medical device vendors often need remote support around the clock; schedule-based or on-request enablement must still work at night, so define who approves after hours. | Medical device vendors sometimes install their own remote access appliance or software; record each one with clinical engineering and route it through the broker where the manufacturer allows.
action_to_2: Inventory vendor connections and require named accounts with MFA (weeks).
action_to_3: Route vendor access through a broker with system-specific access, approval and session logs (two to four months).
action_to_4: Make vendor access just in time with recording and block unapproved remote tools (six months).

question: Is PHI encrypted in transit on internal and external connections?
level_0: External web applications may use TLS, but file transfers, interfaces and internal connections send PHI unencrypted.
level_1: External connections are encrypted; internal HL7 feeds, database connections and printing are unencrypted and not inventoried.
level_2: An inventory of connections carrying PHI exists and external ones are encrypted, but internal interfaces and some legacy protocols remain unencrypted.
level_3: All external connections and internal interfaces carrying PHI use current protocols (for example TLS 1.2 or later), or have documented compensating controls where a vendor cannot support encryption.
target_state: Weak protocols are detected and blocked, certificates are inventoried with expiry alerts, and exceptions are reviewed on a schedule.
evidence: Interface and protocol inventory with encryption status — interface engine and integration team. | TLS configuration scan of external services — vulnerability scanner or external scan report. | Certificate inventory with expiry dates — certificate management or IT operations.
recommended_action: Inventory every connection carrying PHI and encrypt external and internal interfaces, documenting compensating controls where vendors cannot.
probing_questions: Which interfaces send PHI between the EHR, lab, imaging, pharmacy and outside partners, and which of them are encrypted? | Do HL7 feeds through the interface engine use plain transmission on the internal network? | How are files exchanged with payers, clearinghouses and reference labs? | Who tracks certificate expiry for interfaces and web services?
red_flags: The answer covers websites only, not interfaces or file transfers. | Encryption is assumed because traffic stays inside the building.
healthcare_considerations: Many HL7 v2 interfaces use plain transmission on internal networks; adding TLS needs coordination with both application vendors and an interface downtime window. | Some medical devices and older modalities cannot encrypt traffic; place them in restricted segments and record the gap rather than marking the control complete.
action_to_2: Inventory every connection carrying PHI and encrypt external ones (one to two months).
action_to_3: Encrypt internal interfaces and database connections or document compensating controls (three to six months).
action_to_4: Detect weak protocols and alert on certificate expiry (six months).

question: Are email protections (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, attachment and link scanning) enforced?
level_0: No SPF, DKIM or DMARC records, and only basic spam filtering.
level_1: SPF exists, but DKIM is not configured and DMARC is absent or set to monitor only (p=none).
level_2: SPF, DKIM and DMARC exist for the main domain, but DMARC is not at enforcement, other domains are unprotected and attachment or link scanning covers only some mailboxes.
level_3: DMARC is at enforcement (quarantine or reject) for all sending domains, parked domains reject all mail, and attachment and link scanning apply to all mailboxes, with external sender warnings.
target_state: DMARC reports are reviewed regularly, impersonation protection covers executives and finance, users can report phishing in one click, and reported messages are triaged and removed across mailboxes.
evidence: DNS records for SPF, DKIM and DMARC for every owned domain — public DNS lookup. | Email security policy configuration showing attachment and link scanning scope — email security admin portal. | Phishing report and triage records for the last 90 days — security team or email security console.
recommended_action: Move DMARC to enforcement for every domain after aligning third-party senders, and scan attachments and links in all mailboxes.
references: CISA ZTMM v2.0 Applications and Workloads; NIST CSF 2.0 PR.PS
probing_questions: What is the DMARC policy for each domain you own, including old or parked domains? | Which third-party services send mail as your domain (billing, patient portal, appointment reminders), and are they aligned? | Are attachment and link scanning applied to every mailbox, including shared and service mailboxes? | What happens when a user reports a phishing email?
red_flags: DMARC has been at p=none for more than a year. | Scanning policies apply to a pilot group only.
healthcare_considerations: Patient portals, appointment reminder services and billing vendors send mail as the hospital; inventory them before moving DMARC to enforcement so patient communications are not blocked. | Payroll and vendor-payment fraud by email targets finance and revenue cycle staff; add impersonation protection for executives and finance mailboxes.
action_to_2: Publish SPF, DKIM and DMARC for all domains and enable scanning for all mailboxes (weeks).
action_to_3: Move DMARC to quarantine then reject after aligning third-party senders (one to three months).
action_to_4: Review DMARC reports, add impersonation protection and one-click phishing reporting (three months).

question: Is access to applications granted per application based on identity and context, rather than network location?
level_0: Anyone on the internal network or VPN can reach every application's sign-in page and many back-end services.
level_1: A few cloud applications use single sign-on, but on-premises applications trust anyone on the network or VPN.
level_2: Major applications use single sign-on, but access policies do not consider device, location or risk, and VPN users still reach the whole network.
level_3: Critical applications, including EHR remote access, are published through identity-aware access policies that consider user, device and context; network location alone does not grant access.
target_state: All applications use identity-aware access with continuous evaluation, broad VPN access is retired for most users, and policy decisions are logged and reviewed.
evidence: Application list with authentication method (single sign-on, local) — identity provider enterprise applications list. | Access policies with conditions on device and context — identity provider admin portal. | VPN access scope configuration showing which networks users can reach — remote access team.
recommended_action: Publish critical applications, including EHR remote access, through identity-aware policies and limit what VPN users can reach.
references: CISA ZTMM v2.0 Applications and Workloads; NIST CSF 2.0 PR.AA
probing_questions: Once someone is on the VPN, what can they reach? | Which applications use single sign-on, and which still have local passwords? | Do access policies treat a sign-in from an unmanaged device or unusual location differently? | How is the EHR published to remote clinicians?
red_flags: VPN users receive full network access. | Single sign-on exists, but local application accounts remain enabled as a back door.
healthcare_considerations: Many clinical applications are thick clients or vendor-hosted and support only basic authentication; virtual desktop or application gateways can add identity checks in front of them. | Clinicians move between facilities, clinics and home; context policies must allow legitimate after-hours access for on-call staff without blanket exceptions.
action_to_2: Move major applications to single sign-on and limit VPN scope (one to three months).
action_to_3: Publish critical applications through identity-aware policies using device and context (three to six months).
action_to_4: Retire broad VPN access and evaluate access continuously (six to twelve months).

question: Are internet-facing systems and critical applications tested for vulnerabilities at least annually?
level_0: No vulnerability scans or penetration tests have been performed.
level_1: A scan or test happened once, usually for an audit, and findings were not tracked.
level_2: External scans run, but penetration tests are irregular, critical internal applications are not covered and findings are only partly tracked.
level_3: Internet-facing and critical systems receive vulnerability scans at least monthly and a penetration test at least annually, with findings tracked to closure.
target_state: Testing scope follows the inventory and major changes, retests confirm fixes, and results feed the risk register and leadership reporting.
evidence: Most recent penetration test report with scope and finding status — security team. | External vulnerability scan reports for the last three months — scanner or CISA Vulnerability Scanning. | Findings tracker with owners and dates — remediation tracker.
recommended_action: Scan internet-facing systems monthly and penetration-test critical systems annually, tracking every finding to closure.
probing_questions: When was the last penetration test, what was in scope and how many high findings remain open? | Do you know every internet-facing service, including vendor-hosted portals that use your domain? | Are the patient portal, remote access gateways and file transfer services tested? | Who retests findings after they are fixed?
red_flags: The test scope excluded the EHR, remote access or vendor-hosted services. | The same high findings appear in consecutive reports.
healthcare_considerations: Testing live clinical systems and medical devices can disrupt care; agree rules of engagement with clinical leadership and exclude fragile devices from active scanning. | Small hospitals can use free federal services such as CISA external vulnerability scanning to cover internet-facing systems between paid tests.
action_to_2: Scan internet-facing systems monthly, using free CISA scanning if budget is limited (weeks).
action_to_3: Commission an annual penetration test of internet-facing and critical systems and track findings (one quarter).
action_to_4: Tie scope to the inventory and change, retest fixes and report trends (six months).

question: Are vendors required to disclose vulnerabilities and report incidents that affect your systems or data?
level_0: Contracts and business associate agreements do not address vulnerability disclosure or incident reporting beyond the minimum breach notice.
level_1: Business associate agreements require breach notification, but there are no vulnerability disclosure or incident timeframes, and nobody tracks notices.
level_2: New contracts include disclosure and reporting clauses, but older contracts and medical device vendors are not covered and notices are handled ad hoc.
level_3: Contracts for critical vendors require vulnerability disclosure and incident reporting within defined timeframes, and notices are logged, triaged and assigned.
target_state: Vendor notices and advisories are monitored against the inventory, response to each is tracked, and vendor performance is reviewed at renewal.
evidence: Contract and business associate agreement clauses for critical vendors — contracts or legal office. | Log of vendor security notices and actions taken — security or IT operations team. | Subscription list for manufacturer and vendor security advisories — clinical engineering and IT.
recommended_action: Add vulnerability disclosure and incident reporting timeframes to critical vendor contracts and log and triage every vendor notice.
hhs_cpg: CPG-X: Third Party Vulnerability Disclosure; CPG-X: Third Party Incident Reporting
probing_questions: If your EHR or billing vendor had an incident today, how quickly are they required to tell you, and who would receive the notice? | Do your medical device manufacturers provide security advisories and patch guidance, and who reads them? | How many of your critical vendor contracts include incident reporting timeframes? | Show me the last vendor security notice you received and what you did with it.
red_flags: Only business associate agreements are cited, without timeframes. | Notices go to a former employee or a general mailbox no one monitors.
healthcare_considerations: A third-party outage can stop claims, pharmacy or lab results for weeks; incident reporting clauses should include notice of service outages, not only data breaches. | Medical device manufacturers publish security advisories and patch guidance; FDA requires plans to address postmarket vulnerabilities for cyber devices in premarket submissions under section 524B, so ask for them.
action_to_2: Identify critical vendors and the notice requirements in their current contracts (weeks).
action_to_3: Add disclosure and incident reporting timeframes to critical contracts and log every notice (renewal cycle).
action_to_4: Monitor advisories against the inventory and review vendor performance at renewal (ongoing).

question: Is PHI encrypted at rest on servers, endpoints, removable media and backups?
level_0: No encryption at rest on laptops, servers, removable media or backups.
level_1: Some laptops are encrypted, but desktops, servers, USB drives and backups are not, and nobody reports coverage.
level_2: Laptops and most workstations are encrypted, but servers, removable media, backup copies or cloud storage are partly covered, and recovery keys are scattered.
level_3: Encryption at rest covers endpoints, servers, removable media, backups and cloud storage holding PHI, with recovery keys escrowed centrally and coverage reported.
target_state: Encryption coverage is monitored continuously, unencrypted devices are blocked from PHI, removable media is restricted to encrypted devices, and key access is logged.
evidence: Encryption status report for endpoints with recovery key escrow — endpoint management console. | Server, storage and backup encryption settings — storage, backup and cloud admin consoles. | Removable media policy configuration — endpoint management or DLP console.
recommended_action: Encrypt PHI at rest on endpoints, servers, backups, removable media and cloud storage, with central key escrow and coverage reporting.
probing_questions: What percentage of laptops and workstations are encrypted, and where are recovery keys kept? | Are database and file servers, backup copies and cloud storage holding PHI encrypted? | Can staff copy PHI to an unencrypted USB drive? | If you decided encryption was not reasonable for a system, where is that decision documented?
red_flags: Encryption is claimed for laptops only. | Recovery keys are kept on a spreadsheet on a file share.
healthcare_considerations: Workstations on carts and in clinics are easily stolen; HICP lists loss or theft of equipment as one of the main threats to healthcare, and encryption limits the impact. | Medical devices and modalities may store images or results locally without encryption; record them, ask the manufacturer for options and protect them physically.
action_to_2: Encrypt all laptops and workstations and escrow recovery keys centrally (weeks).
action_to_3: Extend encryption to servers, backups, removable media and cloud storage and report coverage (two to four months).
action_to_4: Monitor coverage continuously and block unencrypted devices and media (six months).

question: Is PHI classified and are its storage locations known?
level_0: Nobody knows where PHI is stored outside the EHR.
level_1: The main clinical systems are known, but exports, reports, file shares and cloud storage holding PHI are not mapped.
level_2: A data map lists systems with PHI, but it is incomplete for file shares, cloud storage and departmental databases, and no labels are applied.
level_3: A data map covers applications, file shares, databases and cloud services holding PHI, is reviewed at least annually, and a classification scheme with labels is in use.
target_state: Automated discovery finds PHI in file shares, email and cloud storage, labels are applied automatically where practical, and new locations raise alerts.
evidence: Data map of systems and repositories holding PHI with owners — compliance, privacy or IT. | Classification policy and label usage report — information protection console. | Results of a scan of file shares or cloud storage for PHI — data discovery tool.
recommended_action: Map every system, share and cloud location holding PHI with an owner, and adopt a simple classification scheme with labels.
references: CISA ZTMM v2.0 Data; NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM
probing_questions: Besides the EHR, where do reports and exports with patient data end up (shared drives, spreadsheets, cloud storage, email)? | Which departmental systems (quality, research, case management) hold copies of PHI? | Is there a classification scheme, and do staff use it? | When was the data map last updated, and who owns it?
red_flags: The data map lists only the EHR and billing system. | Labels exist but nobody applies them.
healthcare_considerations: Quality, case management and revenue cycle teams routinely export EHR reports to spreadsheets on shared drives; these exports are often the largest unmanaged store of PHI. | The risk analysis must cover all ePHI the organization creates, receives, maintains or transmits, so the data map is an input to it.
action_to_2: Build a data map of systems and repositories holding PHI with owners (one to two months).
action_to_3: Extend the map to file shares and cloud storage, adopt a classification scheme and review annually (three to six months).
action_to_4: Discover and label PHI automatically and alert on new locations (six to twelve months).

question: Are data loss prevention controls applied to email, cloud storage and endpoints?
level_0: No controls on sending or copying PHI outside the organization.
level_1: Users are told to encrypt sensitive email, but nothing detects or blocks PHI leaving.
level_2: DLP policies exist for email in audit or test mode, or for one channel only; alerts are not reviewed.
level_3: DLP policies for PHI are enforced on email and cloud storage, with defined actions (encrypt, warn, block), and alerts are reviewed by a named owner.
target_state: DLP covers email, cloud storage, endpoints and removable media, policies are tuned using alert data, and incidents feed training and the risk register.
evidence: DLP policy list with mode (test or enforce) and scope — information protection console. | DLP alert and incident report for the last 90 days — information protection console. | Secure external sharing procedure — privacy or IT policy.
recommended_action: Enforce DLP for PHI on email and cloud storage with a secure sharing option and a named alert reviewer.
references: CISA ZTMM v2.0 Data; NIST CSF 2.0 PR.DS
